nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals technical skill and professional respect.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, 'engineer' is a legally protected title in many states, and a licensed one is a 'Professional Engineer' or PE. The word is also used loosely for software and data engineers, and for locomotive engineers on trains. When someone asks 'What do you do?', 'I'm an engineer' is a normal, respected answer.

distinctions.note: A scientist mainly seeks to understand how things work; an engineer applies that knowledge to design and build something useful.
A technician operates or maintains equipment under guidance; an engineer usually designs it and makes decisions about it.

examples.everyday: My brother is a civil engineer, so he always points out bridges and road work when we drive together.
examples.professional: I'm meeting with the platform engineer at two to see whether the data pipeline can handle the new traffic.
examples.analytical: Engineers and scientists often think differently: the engineer must act under uncertainty, while the scientist seeks certainty first.

nuance.analogy: An engineer is the architect of a practical plan, turning a principle into a bridge that carries real traffic.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin ingeniator, from Old French engin, a contrivance; related to engine.
common_mistakes: Saying the word with three even syllables; it is en-juh-NEER with a reduced middle, not 'EN-jin-EER'.
Using 'engineer' for someone who only operates machines; 'operator' or 'technician' is often more accurate in US workplaces.

senses.definition: Relating to enhypostasia.
senses.example: The theologian argued that Christ's human nature is enhypostatic within the divine Person of the Word.

core.definition: In Christian theology, describing a nature, such as Christ's humanity, that has its existence in a divine person (hypostasis) rather than in a separate person of its own.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STAT, the third-to-last syllable of this long word, while the first syllable is secondary. Pronounce the h in 'hypo' clearly and don't reduce the middle vowels into silence.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term of Christian doctrine with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in theology, church history and academic writing about the person of Christ, especially Chalcedonian and Eastern Orthodox Christology. It is not a word for general conversation, so in ordinary speech you would explain the idea in simpler words. Scholars often pair it with 'anhypostatic' when discussing the same doctrine.

distinctions.note: Hypostatic describes the union of the two natures in one person, while enhypostatic describes the human nature's existence within the divine person.
Anhypostatic means having no independent personal existence of its own, which is the negative side of the same doctrine that enhypostatic affirms.

examples.professional: In my seminar paper, I argue that the Chalcedonian language is enhypostatic when it describes Christ's humanity.
examples.analytical: Cyril of Alexandria's account of the Word's union with flesh is enhypostatic: the humanity has no hypostasis of its own, but subsists in the Word.

nuance.analogy: Like a wave that has no separate existence apart from the ocean, the human nature has its existence wholly within the divine person.
nuance.etymology: From Greek en- ('in') plus hypostasis ('underlying reality, substance, person').
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in en-hy-po-STAT-ic versus en-hy-puh-STAT-ik with the same stress pattern; this is a long word that many learners mispronounce.
Confusing it with 'hypostatic', which describes the union of two natures in one person rather than the human nature's dependence on that person.

senses.definition: Angered, made furious, made full of rage.
senses.example: an enraged judge

core.definition: Extremely angry, to the point of losing self-control or acting without thinking.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the only stressed syllable, RAYJ. The -ed ending is not a separate syllable; it blends into the final 'jd' sound, so do not say 'en-RAY-jed'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes intense anger, usually about something unjust or hurtful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enraged for very strong anger, often at a decision, an insult, or an injustice. People often say 'enraged by' or 'enraged at' something. For ordinary annoyance, use 'annoyed', 'upset', or 'mad'. In news writing, enraged is common for crowds or customers.

distinctions.note: Angry is the everyday word and covers everything from mild to strong anger, while enraged marks the highest level.
Furious is about equally strong and more common in speech; enraged suggests anger that has taken over the person's behavior.
Irate is formal and often used for complaints or letters, while enraged is more emotional and describes a person's state.

examples.everyday: My sister was enraged when the airline lost her suitcase on the way home.
examples.professional: Enraged customers flooded the support line after the outage, so we added staff in an hour.
examples.analytical: The crowd, enraged by the verdict, turned a peaceful protest into a violent confrontation.

nuance.analogy: Like a kettle left on high heat, boiling over with no way to release the pressure.
nuance.etymology: From en- and rage, from Old French rage, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, pronouncing it 'en-RAY-jed', rather than one syllable ending in 'jd'.
Using enraged for mild irritation, when annoyed or upset is more natural in American speech.

senses.definition: To make equal; to cause to correspond in amount or degree.
senses.example: to equalize accounts, burdens, or taxes

senses.definition: To clear the ears to balance the pressure in the middle ear with the outside pressure by letting air enter along the Eustachian tubes.
senses.example: Swallowing helps me equalize the pressure in my ears during the descent of the flight.

senses.definition: To precompose with each of a parallel pair of morphisms so as to yield the same composite morphism.
senses.example: In the proof, we equalize the two parallel morphisms by precomposing each with the same map.

senses.definition: To adjust the balance between frequency components within an electronic signal.
senses.example: Before mastering, the engineer will equalize the frequencies in the vocal track.

senses.definition: To make the scoreline equal by scoring points.
senses.example: Late in the second half, Jordan's goal helped equalize the score at two apiece.

core.definition: To make things equal, or to make two things the same in amount, level, or degree.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, "EE," and make the final syllable rhyme with "prize." The middle vowel is a reduced "uh," so say three distinct parts: EE-kwuh-lyze.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it usually describes fairness or correcting an imbalance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell this word equalize, with a z, while British writers often use equalise. In sports, people say "equalize" for tying the score, as in "they equalized in the second half." The term also appears in everyday talk about airplane ears, where you "equalize your ears" by pinching your nose and blowing gently.

distinctions.note: Even out is a casual phrasal verb for making a surface or amount less uneven; equalize is more formal and emphasizes making things the same.
Level usually means to make flat or to flatten a surface; equalize refers to making quantities or chances the same.

examples.everyday: Our team scored late, so we equalized, and the crowd went wild.
examples.professional: We need to equalize the workload across the three teams before the next sprint.
examples.analytical: Public policy aims to equalize opportunity, though critics argue that equal rules can still produce unequal outcomes.

nuance.analogy: To equalize is like balancing a seesaw: you move weight until both sides rest at the same level.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aequalis, "equal," with the English suffix -ize, "to make."
common_mistakes: Spelling it equalise, which is British, when writing for an American audience.
Saying "equalize my ears" without the word "your" in the phrase "equalize your ears".

senses.definition: Capable of being eradicated.
senses.example: Researchers think that polio is an eradicable disease.

core.definition: Able to be completely destroyed or removed at its root, so that it no longer exists or recurs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RAD, the first syllable. The two unstressed vowels are reduced to ih and uh, and the -able ending is a weak syllable, not 'ayb-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a problem as solvable in principle, often in public health, ecology or social policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday talk; they would say 'can be wiped out' or 'can be gotten rid of.' It appears in public health, environmental and policy writing, where it sounds precise and formal. The more common form in speech is the verb 'eradicate' itself.

distinctions.note: Removable means something can be taken away, possibly temporarily, while eradicable means it can be destroyed at its root and not return.
Curable is used for diseases or conditions that can be healed in a patient, while eradicable applies to a disease or pest across a whole population.

examples.professional: The team agreed that the infection is eradicable with a combined vaccine and surveillance program.
examples.analytical: Some prejudices are eradicable through education, but others are so woven into institutions that they seem ineradicable.

nuance.analogy: Like a weed that can be pulled out with its whole root, so it does not grow back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin eradicare, 'to pull out by the root', from ex- 'out' and radix 'root'.
common_mistakes: Confusing eradicable with ineradicable, which means 'cannot be eradicated.'
Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first syllable, RAD.

senses.definition: In an erect manner.

core.definition: In an upright, straight position, with the body or an object standing or sitting straight up.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the stressed root, REKT, and keep the -ly ending short and light. Do not add an extra vowel between the k and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes posture or position without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in conversation. They say 'sit up straight', 'stand up straight', or 'upright' instead. You will meet 'erectly' mainly in medical descriptions, formal writing, or fiction describing posture.

distinctions.note: 'Upright' is the everyday American word and works as both adjective and adverb, while 'erectly' sounds formal or literary.
'Straight' is common in speech, as in 'sit straight', while 'erectly' emphasizes a stiff, vertical posture.

examples.professional: The presenter stood erectly at the front of the room while she walked us through the dashboard.
examples.analytical: The sculpture depicts a figure standing erectly, which signals a moral stability the poem's narrator lacks.

nuance.analogy: Like a flagpole standing straight in still air.
nuance.etymology: From Latin erectus, past participle of erigere 'to raise up', plus the English adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'erectly' in casual speech, where 'upright' or 'sit up straight' sounds more natural.
Stressing the second syllable or adding an extra vowel between the k and t.

senses.definition: In a special manner; specially.
senses.example: He got up early especially.

senses.definition: Particularly; to a greater extent than is normal.
Exceptionally.
senses.example: The buildings are not especially large.

senses.definition: Used to place greater emphasis upon someone or something.
senses.example: Invite them all, especially Molly.

core.definition: To a greater degree than usual or than other things; particularly, or in particular.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPESH, and the ending is often reduced to 'ih-SPESH-lee' in fast speech. Do not say 'ess-PEH-shuh-lee' with stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it adds emphasis and is used for both praise and concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use especially constantly in speech and writing, for example to highlight one example from a list or to show a reason, as in 'especially because it is raining.' It can also introduce a disclaimer such as 'not especially' to mean 'not very much.' Its meaning is close to particularly, though especially often feels a little warmer.

distinctions.note: Specially means for a particular purpose, as in 'I made this specially for you,' while especially means to a high degree or in particular.
The two are close in meaning, but particularly is slightly more neutral and analytical, while especially is more common in speech.

examples.everyday: The coffee here is great, especially the cold brew in summer.
examples.professional: The model struggles with rare categories, especially when the classes are highly imbalanced.
examples.analytical: Kant's account of duty becomes especially difficult to apply when two obligations conflict.

nuance.analogy: Especially is like a highlighter on a page: it does not change the text, but it makes one part stand out to the reader.
nuance.etymology: Formed from especial plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing especially with specially: 'I made it specially for you' is correct, not 'especially for you'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'ess-PESH-ly', instead of the stress on the second syllable with a reduced ending.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to euphemism.
senses.example: Calling the layoffs rightsizing was a euphemistic way to avoid saying people lost their jobs.

core.definition: Using a mild or indirect word or phrase in place of a blunter one, often to soften or hide an unpleasant fact.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MIS, the third syllable. The first 'eu' is 'yoo', and the ending is 'tik', not 'tick' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative; it describes softened language that may be polite or evasive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'euphemistic' in writing, teaching and commentary about language, such as 'euphemistic language in the report'. In casual talk people would more often say 'soft', 'polite' or 'a nicer way to say it'. It can suggest that the language is dishonest, so use it with care when describing someone's words.

distinctions.note: Polite describes manners in general; euphemistic describes specific word choices that replace a blunt term.
Vague means unclear; euphemistic language is clear enough but softened on purpose.

examples.everyday: Saying 'let go' instead of 'fired' sounds a little euphemistic, but it is kinder.
examples.professional: The memo's euphemistic language about 'rightsizing' hid the fact that people were losing their jobs.
examples.analytical: The euphemistic phrasing of the report obscures who is responsible for the decision.

nuance.analogy: Euphemistic language is like a frosted window: you can still see the shape, but the details are blurred.
nuance.etymology: From euphemism, from Greek euphēmismos, 'use of words of good omen', plus the adjective suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Using it as a noun; the noun is 'euphemism'.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the third.

senses.definition: To leave or withdraw from; to quit; to retire from.
senses.example: The soldiers evacuated the fortress.

senses.definition: To cause (or help) to leave or withdraw from.
senses.example: The firefighters decided to evacuate all the inhabitants from the street.

senses.definition: To make empty; to empty out; to remove the contents of, including to create a vacuum.
senses.example: The scientist evacuated the chamber before filling it with nitrogen.

senses.definition: To make empty; to deprive.
senses.example: The budget cuts evacuated the department of nearly all its funding.

senses.definition: To remove; to eject; to void; to discharge, as the contents of a vessel, or of the bladder or the bowels (to stool).
senses.example: The nurse evacuated the catheter bag every hour and recorded the output.

senses.definition: To make void; to nullify; to vacate.
senses.example: to evacuate a contract or marriage

core.definition: To leave a place quickly and in an organized way, or to move people out of a place, usually because of danger such as fire, flood, or a storm.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable, VAK. The 'ua' in 'evacuate' is said as 'yoo', and the final '-ate' is pronounced 'ayt'. Do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it suggests an urgent or serious situation. In everyday talk it carries the weight of real danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evacuate for official orders during fires, hurricanes, chemical leaks, or bomb threats, and the phrase 'mandatory evacuation' is common in news reports. In casual speech people more often say 'get out' or 'leave', but 'evacuate' is the right word for organized movement of a group. Using it for a simple move to a new apartment would sound odd.

distinctions.note: Escape means getting away from danger yourself, often without help or planning, while evacuate usually describes an organized movement of people or a group.
Vacate means leaving a room, seat, or property, often for ordinary reasons, and does not necessarily imply danger or emergency.

examples.everyday: The fire alarm went off, so everyone had to evacuate the apartment building and wait in the parking lot.
examples.professional: Facilities asked us to evacuate the office during the gas leak drill, so please gather at the north gate.
examples.analytical: Whether a government should evacuate a city before a hurricane depends on balancing the risk to lives against the economic and psychological costs of displacement.

nuance.analogy: Evacuating is like emptying a boat before it sinks: everyone is moved out in an orderly way so no one is left behind.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'evacuare', meaning 'to empty out', from 'ex-' (out) and 'vacuus' (empty).
common_mistakes: Using 'evacuate' for an ordinary move, which sounds dramatic
Confusing 'evacuate' with 'vacate' when the situation involves no danger
Pronouncing the middle as 'vac-you-ate' with a separate syllable for each vowel instead of the smoother 'VAK-yoo-ayt'

evacuate.etymology: Latin *ēvacuātus*, the perfect passive participle of *ēvacuō* (“to empty out, evacuate”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: The Christian gospel.
A salutary principle relating to morals, politics, etc.
senses.example: Her father's evangel of honesty and hard work shaped every decision she made.

senses.definition: An evangelist.
senses.example: The old evangel preached in the town square every Sunday, drawing crowds from across the county.

core.definition: The Christian gospel, meaning the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ, or a message that announces such good news.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VAN. The 'g' is said as a soft 'j' sound, and the final '-el' is a light syllable, close to 'juhl'. Do not pronounce the ending as 'gel'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a sincere, important message, usually in religious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'evangel' in everyday speech. You will meet it in sermons, theology, and literary writing, where it can sound formal or old-fashioned. In ordinary conversation people say 'the gospel' or 'the good news'.

distinctions.note: Gospel is the common word in American church life, while evangel is more literary and rarely used outside formal or poetic writing.
An evangel is the message itself, while an evangelist is a person who proclaims it.

examples.everyday: At the potluck, the pastor's wife said the evangel was the reason their church started the food pantry.
examples.professional: Our denomination's curriculum for new members stresses that the evangel should shape every program, not only the Sunday service.
examples.analytical: In Paul's letters, the evangel is not a set of moral instructions but an announcement about what God has already done in Christ.

nuance.analogy: An evangel is like a herald's proclamation in an old kingdom: it is a message of good news that everyone is meant to hear and pass on.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'euangelion', meaning 'good news', from 'eu' (good) and 'angelos' (messenger).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'gel' rather than 'juhl'
Using 'evangel' in casual conversation where 'gospel' or 'good news' is more natural
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word 'euangelion' (good news, gospel) is the source of this word. In the RSV, Mark 1:1 introduces Jesus' ministry as the beginning of the good news about him. Mark 1:14-15 describes Jesus preaching the good news of God and calling people to repent and believe it. Romans 1:16 says Paul is not ashamed of the gospel because it is the power of God for salvation.

evangel.etymology: From Middle English *evaungel*, *evangile*, from Old French *evangile*, from Late Latin *evangelium*, from Ancient Greek *εὐαγγέλιον* (“good news”), from *εὐάγγελος* (“bringing good news”), from *εὐ-* (“well”) + *ἀγγέλλειν* (“to announce”) (English *angel*).

senses.definition: Remaining calm even in situations that would cause many others to become angry, frustrated, panicky, etc.
senses.example: My even-tempered manager stayed calm even when the server crashed during launch.

core.definition: Remaining calm and steady in mood, not easily angered, frustrated, or upset, even in difficult situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TEMP, the second part. The -ered ending is weak, sounding like erd. Keep even short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises calm, reliable temperament in people, pets, and coworkers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use even-tempered to describe a person or animal's steady temperament: 'Our new dog is really even-tempered.' It is common in conversation, job descriptions, and reviews. Use it for a long-term trait, not a single moment. A natural reply is 'That's great, we need that around here.'

distinctions.note: Even-keeled emphasizes steadiness through changing conditions. Even-tempered emphasizes a naturally calm disposition.
Patient describes willingness to wait or tolerate delay. Even-tempered describes emotional steadiness generally.

examples.everyday: Our new neighbor's dog is so even-tempered that the kids can play with him all day.
examples.professional: We need an even-tempered project manager who stays calm when the client escalates.
examples.analytical: Interpreters of Aristotle's ethics often describe the well-ordered person as even-tempered, feeling anger neither too quickly nor too little.

nuance.analogy: Like a thermostat that holds the room at a steady temperature no matter what happens outside.
nuance.etymology: Temper comes from Latin temperare, meaning to mix in due proportion.
common_mistakes: Writing it without a hyphen, as in even tempered.
Confusing it with temperate, which describes moderation in habits or climate, not mood.

senses.definition: In a manner relating to evolution or slow development.
senses.example: Evolutionarily, our brains have been shaped by long periods of scarcity and social cooperation.

senses.definition: From the perspective of evolution.

core.definition: In terms of evolution; through or from the standpoint of natural selection and gradual change over generations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOO, with a lighter secondary stress on NAIR, and the ending -ly is 'lee' with a reduced vowel. Do not stress the final syllable, as in 'ev-uh-loo-shuh-nair-uh-LEE'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical description rather than an emotional word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evolutionarily mainly in biology, psychology, anthropology and academic writing, for example when explaining why a trait might persist. In casual talk people more often say from an evolutionary standpoint or evolutionarily speaking. The word can sound jargon-heavy, so use it when precision matters.

distinctions.note: Evolutionary is the adjective, as in an evolutionary advantage; evolutionarily is the adverb modifying an adjective or verb, as in evolutionarily successful.
Biologically means in terms of the body or living systems in general; evolutionarily refers specifically to long-term change through natural selection.

examples.everyday: Evolutionarily speaking, we're wired to notice snakes faster than we notice most other things.
examples.professional: The algorithm is evolutionarily inspired, so it tests many variants and keeps the ones that score best.
examples.analytical: Some ethicists argue that moral intuitions are evolutionarily shaped, which raises the question of whether they are reliable guides to truth.

nuance.analogy: Calling a trait evolutionarily old is like reading a building's foundation: it tells you the history beneath what you see now.
nuance.etymology: Formed from evolutionary plus the adverb suffix -ly; evolution comes from Latin evolutio 'an unrolling'.
common_mistakes: Using evolutionarily where you need the adjective evolutionary before a noun, as in 'an evolutionarily advantage'.
Stressing the last syllable instead of LOO.

senses.definition: To an excessive degree.
senses.example: The application form was excessively complicated.

senses.definition: In excess.
senses.example: He smoked excessively.

core.definition: To a degree that is more than is reasonable, necessary, or healthy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -SES-. The first vowel is reduced to a short 'ih' sound, and the final -ly is pronounced 'lee,' not 'lie.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually signals a problem, such as too much of something that is bad or costly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use excessively mostly in writing, reports, and formal speech, as in 'excessively expensive' or 'excessively noisy.' In casual talk people more often say way too or really. It can sound stiff in a friendly conversation, so use it there only for emphasis or a complaint.

distinctions.note: Extremely describes a high degree neutrally, while excessively implies more than is reasonable or acceptable.
Too is common in speech and means more than is needed or wanted; excessively is more formal and stresses the degree.

examples.everyday: The hotel charged excessively high prices for bottled water, so we just bought some at the grocery store.
examples.professional: The dashboard refresh is excessively slow, so please check whether the query is scanning the whole table.
examples.analytical: A theory that explains everything by appeal to hidden causes is excessively flexible, and that flexibility makes it untestable.

nuance.analogy: Excessively is like adding too much salt to soup: a little brings out the flavor, but excessively ruins the whole pot.
nuance.etymology: From excessive plus the adverb suffix -ly; excessive comes from Latin excessus, 'going beyond.'
common_mistakes: Using excessively for positive things, where very or extremely is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable as 'SEE-siv' instead of 'SES-iv.'

senses.definition: In an expansive manner.

core.definition: In a broad, generous or sweeping way; with open, enthusiastic gestures or speech.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPAN, and the ending -ively is said as siv-lee with a reduced first syllable. Do not add an extra syllable in the -ly ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, suggesting generosity, breadth or open enthusiasm, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use expansively in casual speech. You will see it in writing and formal narration, for example to describe someone gesturing expansively or talking expansively about plans. In conversation people more often say with a sweeping gesture or with enthusiasm.

distinctions.note: Enthusiastically focuses on eagerness; expansively focuses on breadth, sweeping gestures or wide-ranging talk.
Extensively refers to thoroughness or amount; expansively suggests a generous, open manner.

examples.everyday: He gestured expansively toward the lake as he described how the house used to look.
examples.professional: She described the roadmap expansively, though the timeline itself was still vague.
examples.analytical: Kant writes expansively about reason, yet his main claims depend on a small set of carefully stated premises.

nuance.analogy: Like someone spreading their arms wide to show you how big a fish was.
nuance.etymology: From expansive plus -ly, from Latin expandere, to spread out.
common_mistakes: Using expansively to mean extensively or thoroughly in technical writing; it refers to manner, not extent.
Placing the stress on the last syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: To set out the meaning of; to explain or discuss at length.
senses.example: Today I'll expound at length the theory propounded last week.

senses.definition: To make a statement, especially at length.
senses.example: He expounded often on the dangers of the imperial presidency.

core.definition: To explain or set out the meaning of something in detail, or to discuss a topic at length.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SPOWND. The final d is clearly pronounced, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful, detailed explanation, often of a difficult idea or text.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expound mostly in writing, academic talk, sermons, or formal discussion, not in casual conversation. The common pattern is 'expound on' or 'expound upon' a topic, as in 'She expounded on her theory for an hour.' In everyday speech, 'explain' or 'go into detail' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Explain is everyday and neutral; expound implies a longer, more systematic, and often more formal treatment.
Elaborate means to add more detail to what was already said; expound means to set out a fuller account of an idea from the start.

examples.everyday: My uncle loves to expound on the history of every town we drive through.
examples.professional: Before we vote, let me expound on the risks of changing the database schema.
examples.analytical: Aquinas expounds the distinction between essence and existence with remarkable precision.

nuance.analogy: If explaining is walking someone across a room, expounding is giving them a full guided tour of the entire building.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English expounen, from Latin exponere, 'to set out', from ex- 'out' plus ponere 'to put'.
common_mistakes: Using expound without 'on' or 'upon' when a topic follows, as in 'expound the topic' instead of 'expound on the topic' (the direct object form is fine with a doctrine or meaning).
Using expound for a short, simple explanation, which sounds stiff.

expound.etymology: From Middle English *expounden*, from Old French *espondre*, from Latin *expono*.

senses.definition: Excessive or superfluous expenditure of money.
Prodigality, as of anger, love, expression, imagination, or demands.
senses.example: Her extravagance in praising the new restaurant embarrassed the chef, who had heard it all before.

senses.definition: Something extravagant; something done out of extravagance.
senses.example: That luxury car is an extravagance you can't afford.

core.definition: Spending too much money or resources on things you do not need; also, an expensive item bought for pleasure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STRAV. The middle syllables reduce to a schwa, and the final '-ance' sounds like 'uns', not 'ants'.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral; it usually implies waste or excess, though a small treat can be called a fun extravagance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to criticize spending: 'That's an extravagance we can't afford.' It can also be affectionate, as in 'a little extravagance.' Informal alternatives include 'splurge' and 'treat'.

distinctions.note: Luxury describes high-end comfort; extravagance stresses spending beyond what is reasonable.
Splurge is informal and usually a one-time treat; extravagance can describe a general habit or a sharp excess.
Waste is using something uselessly; extravagance is spending freely on luxuries, though the two can overlap.

examples.everyday: Buying the fancy espresso machine was a bit of an extravagance, but I love it.
examples.professional: Approving that conference trip at this stage would be an extravagance we can't justify.
examples.analytical: Thoreau criticized the extravagance of American consumer habits, arguing that luxuries often bind people more than they free them.

nuance.analogy: Like a dessert cart at a diner: tempting and sweet, but a choice that goes beyond what you need.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extravagans, 'wandering outside', from extra 'outside' and vagari 'to wander'.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'extravigance'; the root vowel is a.
Using it for a general excess of feeling; it is mainly about money and resources.

core.definition: A Hebrew name meaning help; several Old Testament men bear it, including a repairer of Jerusalem's wall.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EE. The final -er is a reduced, unstressed vowel, close to the r sound of the word er.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a name used in Bible study and religious discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Ezer mainly in Bible study, sermons and religious conversation. You would say it when reading Nehemiah or discussing the Hebrew word for helper in Genesis 2:18. It is rare in casual talk, and people usually pronounce it the same way in every setting.
word_family: ezer kenegdo (Hebrew phrase, a helper suitable for him)

distinctions.note: Ezra is a different and more prominent biblical figure, a priest and scribe; Ezer is a name shared by several less prominent men.

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader said Ezer is also a Hebrew word for help.
examples.professional: In our curriculum on Hebrew names, we noted that Ezer appears several times in Chronicles and Nehemiah.
examples.analytical: The name Ezer, meaning help, links semantically with the phrase ezer kenegdo in Genesis 2:18, though the men who bear the name are distinct.

nuance.analogy: Like a common surname shared by several people in one town, Ezer names several different men in the Bible.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew word 'ezer, meaning help or helper.
common_mistakes: Confusing Ezer with Ezra, who is a different and more prominent figure.
Saying EZ-er; the American pronunciation is EE-zer.
nuance.biblical_note: Ezer is the Hebrew word for help, used in Genesis 2:18 for the woman as a helper suitable for the man. The name Ezer belongs to several men: Ezer son of Ephraim in 1 Chronicles 7:21, Ezer the Horite in Genesis 36:21, and Ezer who helped repair part of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah 3:19. Each appears briefly, and the name's meaning highlights divine help rather than one prominent role.

senses.definition: A meeting, especially a meeting between two people conducted in person as opposed to a meeting conducted at a distance through technology.
In one another's presence.
senses.example: a face-to-face meeting

senses.definition: While physically present.

core.definition: Happening in person, with people physically present together, rather than by phone, video or text.

pronunciation.tip: The second 'face' gets the main stress, and the 'to' is reduced to 'tuh'. Say 'fayss-tuh-FAYSS', with the first 'face' lighter.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, suggesting openness and direct contact. In the sense of a confrontation, it can suggest tension.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use face-to-face in work and personal life when they want a serious conversation in person, as in 'Let's talk face-to-face.' It is common in meetings, relationships and sales. A natural reply is 'Sure, when are you free?' In everyday speech, in person is equally common and sometimes more natural.

distinctions.note: In person is more common in everyday American speech and means the same thing, while face-to-face can sound slightly more formal or emphatic.
Remote describes work or communication done at a distance, often by video or phone, which is the opposite of face-to-face contact.

examples.everyday: I'd rather have a face-to-face talk about it than go back and forth by text.
examples.professional: Let's hold a face-to-face meeting with the vendor before we sign the contract.
examples.analytical: Paul's contrast between partial knowledge now and seeing face to face later raises questions about the nature of divine vision.

nuance.analogy: A face-to-face meeting is like handing someone a letter directly instead of sending it through the mail: the message arrives with all its tone and body language.
nuance.etymology: From face, from Latin facies, plus to, plus face, meaning two people looking directly at each other.
common_mistakes: Using face-to-face with the wrong preposition, as in 'face-to-face with the team' when the context is 'in a face-to-face meeting with the team'.
Writing 'face to face' without hyphens in attributive position, as in 'a face to face meeting', which is less standard than 'a face-to-face meeting'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Greek, 1 Corinthians 13:12 uses prosopon pros prosopon, literally face to face, to describe a fuller seeing of God after this life. Exodus 33:11 describes the LORD speaking with Moses in a close and intimate way. Genesis 32:30 records Jacob saying he has seen God face to face and yet his life has been preserved.

traditions.view: Orthodox Christians understand the face-to-face vision of God in terms of participation in God's energies rather than direct sight of God's essence, which remains beyond creaturely comprehension. Saints are said to behold God in this sense.
Roman Catholic teaching describes the beatific vision as the immediate, face-to-face sight of God's essence granted to the blessed after death, as defined in the 1336 constitution Benedictus Deus.

Most Protestant traditions affirm that believers will see God face to face in glory, though Lutherans and Reformed Christians differ on how far creatures can grasp God's essence, with many Reformed writers stressing God's incomprehensibility.

senses.definition: A flourish of trumpets or horns as to announce; a short and lively air performed on hunting horns during the chase.
senses.example: They played a short fanfare to announce the arrival of the king.

senses.definition: A show of ceremony or celebration.
senses.example: The town opened the new library with fanfare and a speech from the mayor.

senses.definition: To play a fanfare.
senses.example: The brass section fanfared as the governor walked onto the stage.

senses.definition: To imitate a fanfare, in order to dramatize the presentation or introduction of something.
senses.example: The trailer's synthesizers fanfare each dramatic reveal to build suspense for the film.

senses.definition: To introduce with pomp and show.
senses.example: The company fanfared its new smartphone with a glitzy launch party in Manhattan.

senses.definition: To mark an arrival or departure with music, noise, or drama.
senses.example: Church bells fanfared the bride and groom as they stepped out into the sunshine.

senses.definition: To publicize or announce.
senses.example: The museum fanfared its reopening on social media and in the local newspapers.

senses.definition: To fan out.
senses.example: Search teams fanfared outward from the crash site across the snowy ridge.

senses.definition: To embellish with fanfares.
senses.example: The jeweler fanfared the storefront windows with gold ribbons and sparkling lights.

core.definition: A short, loud flourish of trumpets or horns played to announce something important, or a showy public celebration.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FAN, and make the final -are a clear American r. Say 'FAN-fair,' not 'fan-FAHR.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral, suggesting celebration; it can also imply excessive showiness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fanfare in news and everyday talk, especially in phrases like 'with great fanfare' or 'without fanfare.' It is not an interjection or casual word, but it is common in news, business, and ordinary conversation. A natural reply to 'Was the opening big?' might be, 'No, it opened with almost no fanfare.'

distinctions.note: Hoopla is informal and suggests overhyped commotion, while fanfare is more formal and describes a celebration or announcement.
Publicity is the attention generated by media or promotion, while fanfare is the ceremonial or showy display itself.
Ceremony is the formal ritual, while fanfare is the loud, celebratory display that often accompanies it.

examples.everyday: The new coffee shop opened last week with almost no fanfare, but the line was out the door by noon.
examples.professional: We'll launch the feature quietly, with no press fanfare, so we can watch the metrics first.
examples.analytical: Scholars note that the monarchy's public entrances relied on fanfare to make power visible to people who could never see the ruler up close.

nuance.analogy: Fanfare is like the drumroll before a magic trick: the noise announces that something important is about to happen.
nuance.etymology: From French fanfare, probably imitative of the sound of trumpets; origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using fanfare for any party; it refers to a loud or ceremonial display, not a quiet gathering.
Saying 'with no fanfare' in a way that sounds stiff; 'without fanfare' is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable (fan-FAIR).

senses.definition: To evoke an intense interest or attraction in someone.
senses.example: The flickering TV fascinated the cat.

senses.definition: To make someone hold motionless; to spellbind.
senses.example: We were fascinated by the potter's skill.

senses.definition: To be irresistibly charming or attractive to.
senses.example: Her gait fascinates all men.

core.definition: To attract and hold someone's strong interest or attention so completely that they can hardly look away.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the middle syllables short and quick. The final -ate is pronounced ayt, not uht.

nuance.connotation: Positive; describes strong interest or enchantment, though it can sound slightly negative when it means controlling attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fascinate in conversation and writing, but it is stronger than interest, so people often say I find it fascinating or I'm fascinated by. The person is usually the one who is fascinated, and the subject is what fascinates. Saying something fascinates you can sound emotional, so use it when you really mean captivated.

distinctions.note: Interest is the general word for attention to something, while fascinate means holding someone's attention so strongly it feels almost irresistible.
Intrigue suggests curiosity about a mystery that makes you want to know more, while fascinate is about being captivated.

examples.everyday: The documentary about deep-sea creatures really fascinated my kids.
examples.professional: The new dashboard fascinated the executives, but they asked for clearer metrics before approving it.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long been fascinated by how a conscious mind can represent a world it never directly perceives.

nuance.analogy: Like a magnet that pulls your attention in and will not let go.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fascinare, meaning to bewitch or enchant, from fascinum, meaning charm or spell.
common_mistakes: Saying I am fascinating when you mean you are interested; use I am fascinated for the feeling.
Using fascinated for or fascinated with; fascinated by is the most common American preposition.

fascinate.etymology: Latin *fascinātus*, perfect passive participle of *fascinō* (“to enchant, bewitch, fascinate”) (see *-ate*), from *fascinum* (“a phallus-shaped amulet worn around the neck in Ancient Rome; witchcraft”) + *-ō*, itself of obscure origin.

senses.definition: A weariness caused by exertion; exhaustion.
senses.example: After the twelve-hour shift, a deep fatigue settled over the nurses as they walked to their cars.

senses.definition: A menial task or tasks, especially in the military.
senses.example: Recruits spent their first week on fatigue duty, scrubbing latrines and peeling potatoes in the mess hall.

senses.definition: Weakening and eventual failure of material, typically by cracking leading to complete separation, caused by repeated application of mechanical stress to the material.
senses.example: Engineers found that metal fatigue, not corrosion, caused the bridge's support beam to crack.

senses.definition: Attributive form of fatigues (“military clothing worn when doing menial tasks”).
senses.example: He pulled on his fatigue jacket before heading out to the motor pool at dawn.

senses.definition: To tire or make weary by physical or mental exertion.
senses.example: Long hours of lifting boxes began to fatigue his lower back and shoulders.

senses.definition: To wilt a salad by dressing or tossing it.
senses.example: Pour the warm bacon dressing over the spinach to fatigue the leaves slightly.

senses.definition: To lose so much strength or energy that one becomes tired, weary, feeble or exhausted.
senses.example: By the third hour of the marathon, she began to fatigue noticeably on the hills.

senses.definition: To undergo the process of fatigue; to fail as a result of fatigue.
senses.example: After thousands of cycles, the aluminum bracket began to fatigue and finally snapped.

senses.definition: To cause to undergo the process of fatigue.
senses.example: The repeated pressurization cycles fatigued the airplane's metal skin until it eventually broke up in flight.

core.definition: A state of extreme tiredness caused by physical or mental effort, lack of sleep, or long stress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TEEG, and make the final sound a hard g, not a j. The first vowel is a weak schwa, so say 'fuh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it describes a condition that needs rest, though it can be used in neutral technical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'fatigue' in health discussions, workplace conversations and technical writing. In casual talk people often say 'I'm exhausted' or 'I'm wiped out'. 'Fatigue' is also used for materials that weaken under repeated stress, such as metal, and for decision making that has worn people down.

distinctions.note: Tiredness is the common everyday word; fatigue is more formal and suggests a deeper, more persistent exhaustion.
Exhaustion is stronger and means complete depletion of energy; fatigue can be milder or ongoing.

examples.everyday: I've had so much fatigue lately from working nights that I can barely stay awake.
examples.professional: The alerts are causing alarm fatigue on the operations team, so we need to reduce the noise.
examples.analytical: Weber distinguishes fatigue from the wider sense of moral exhaustion that marks the modern worker.

nuance.analogy: Fatigue is like a rubber band bent back and forth until it finally weakens and snaps.
nuance.etymology: From French fatiguer, from Latin fatigare, 'to tire out'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'FAT-ig'; the stress falls on the second syllable.
Pronouncing the final sound as a j instead of a hard g.

fatigue.etymology: From French *fatigue*, from *fatiguer*, from Latin *fatīgō* (“to weary, tire, vex, harass”).

senses.definition: The state, quality, or condition of being fat.

core.definition: The condition of having a large amount of body fat, or the quality of being fat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FAT. The ending -ness is a short, unstressed 'nus', not a long 'nes'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or sensitive; it can sound judgmental when used about a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use fatness in casual conversation about people, because it can sound blunt or insulting. Everyday speech prefers weight, body size, or a more neutral phrase. Fatness appears more often in research, health discussions, and debates about body image.

distinctions.note: Obesity is a clinical term based on a measure such as body mass index, while fatness is a more general description of body fat.
Weight is a neutral measurement of mass, while fatness specifically refers to body fat and carries more judgment.

examples.everyday: People sometimes judge someone's health by their fatness alone, and that is not fair.
examples.professional: Our study measured body fatness with DEXA scans rather than relying only on body mass index.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers often treated fatness as a sign of prosperity, while modern medicine reads it as a risk factor.

nuance.analogy: Like the amount of ink in a pen: it describes how much is inside, not how the pen is shaped.
nuance.etymology: From fat plus the suffix -ness, from Old English fætt, fat.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as a long nes sound, as in FAT-nes.
Using fatness to describe a person in casual talk, which sounds rude; choose weight or body size instead.

fatness.etymology: From Middle English *fatnesse*, *fattenesse*, from Old English *fǣtnes* (“fatness, the richest part of anything”), equivalent to *fat* + *-ness*.

senses.definition: Having or displaying faults; not perfect; not adequate or acceptable.
senses.example: They replaced the faulty wiring and it has worked fine ever since.

core.definition: Not working properly, or not meeting standards, because of defects or errors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the l is light before the t. The second syllable is a clear 'tee' with a long e, not a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it indicates something is defective or unreliable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'faulty' for products, wiring, brakes, memory, and reasoning, as in 'faulty wiring' or 'faulty logic.' It is neutral enough for everyday talk and standard in customer service and safety contexts. For a stronger, more formal word for products that fail to meet standards, Americans often say 'defective.'

distinctions.note: Defective is more formal and often used for products that fail to meet specifications or are subject to recalls, while faulty is broader and more everyday.
Broken means not working at all, while faulty means it works badly or unreliably.
Flawed often describes a plan, argument, or design with an imperfection, while faulty more often describes a working part or a conclusion based on an error.

examples.everyday: The smoke detector is faulty, because it keeps chirping at night.
examples.professional: The alert was triggered by a faulty sensor, so we are not treating it as a real outage yet.
examples.analytical: The argument is valid in form, but its conclusion rests on a faulty premise about human motivation.

nuance.analogy: A faulty map with a few wrong roads is still useful in general, but you cannot trust it at every turn.
nuance.etymology: From fault and the suffix -y, from Old French faute, meaning a failing.
common_mistakes: Confusing faulty with faultless; 'faulty' means it has problems, while 'faultless' means it has none.
Using faulty for a person without a clear sense of defect, where 'mistaken' or 'wrong' is more natural.

senses.definition: US standard spelling of favorite.
US standard spelling of favorite.
US standard spelling of favorite.

core.definition: Liked more than others; or, in sports or competition, expected to win.

pronunciation.tip: Say it in two quick syllables with stress on FAY, and reduce the middle to 'ver' so it sounds like 'FAY-vrit.' Many learners say three full syllables, but Americans usually blend the middle one.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses preference and affection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'favorite' constantly in everyday speech, such as 'What's your favorite color?' As an adjective it comes before the noun. In sports, 'the favorite' means the team or player most likely to win, and 'the favorites' is common in betting and news. You can also use it as a noun or verb, but the adjective is most common in conversation.

distinctions.note: Preferred sounds more formal and business-like, as in 'our preferred vendor,' while favorite is warm and everyday.
Best describes quality, while favorite describes personal liking, so a favorite may not be the best.

examples.everyday: My favorite restaurant is the little taco place near our house.
examples.professional: Our favorite approach for the migration is to move one service at a time.
examples.analytical: The author's favorite example of moral choice reveals the assumptions underlying her entire argument.

nuance.analogy: A favorite is like the chair you always reach for in a room: it is the one you prefer over the rest.
nuance.etymology: From Italian favorito, past participle of favorire, to favor.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as three full syllables, 'FAY-vor-ite,' instead of the reduced two-syllable American form.
Using 'favorite' with 'the most' in front, as in 'the most favorite,' which is ungrammatical.

conversation.text: The Chiefs are the favorites to win it all.
They were the big favorite, but they lost.
What's your favorite team? You're from Boston, right?

senses.definition: In a fearless manner; without fear.

core.definition: In a way that shows no fear; boldly and without hesitation, even in dangerous or difficult situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FEER. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the ending -ly is a clear long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises courage and directness, though it can sound dramatic when used for small things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fearlessly to praise someone who speaks up or acts boldly, as in 'she fearlessly questioned the plan.' It is common in news, sports and business writing. Casual speakers often use 'boldly' or 'without hesitation' instead.

distinctions.note: Bravely implies someone felt fear and acted anyway, while fearlessly implies no fear was felt at all.
Boldly stresses confidence and visibility, while fearlessly stresses the absence of fear.

examples.everyday: My daughter fearlessly jumped into the pool on her first try.
examples.professional: During the review, she fearlessly flagged the flaws in our model and proposed a better validation method.
examples.analytical: The prophet fearlessly confronts the king, trusting that the truth of God's word matters more than his own safety.

nuance.analogy: Fearlessly is like a child who runs toward the waves without checking for danger, simply not registering fear.
nuance.etymology: From fearless and the suffix -ly, in the manner of.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as 'fear-LESS-ly'.
Using fearlessly for ordinary bravery where bravely fits better.

core.definition: Autumn Jewish festival (Sukkot) when people lived in temporary booths to remember the wilderness years and thank God for the harvest.

pronunciation.tip: Feast of is said quickly as feest uv, with a weak v sound, not 'of' like 'off'. The main stress falls on the NAK syllable of tabernacles.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It carries religious meaning and joy, and it is used respectfully in Jewish and Christian contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name mainly in religious settings, Bible study, sermons, and conversations about Jewish holidays. Many people refer to it as Sukkot when speaking with Jewish friends. Its name comes from the English word tabernacle, a tent or dwelling place, not a church building.

distinctions.note: Passover commemorates the Exodus and falls in spring; Tabernacles falls in autumn and remembers the wilderness years.
Weeks is a late-spring festival about the grain harvest; Tabernacles is an autumn harvest festival marked by living in booths.

collocations: build a booth for the Feast

examples.everyday: Our Jewish neighbors are building a little booth in their backyard for the Feast of Tabernacles.
examples.professional: In my sermon series, I connect Jesus' teaching in John 7 to the Feast of Tabernacles.
examples.analytical: Zechariah 14 pictures the nations going up each year to keep the Feast of Tabernacles, linking the festival to the future reign of God.

nuance.analogy: Like a family spending a week in a backyard tent each fall to remember a hard journey and give thanks for food.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew sukkot, plural of sukkah, booth or hut; English tabernacle comes from Latin tabernaculum, tent.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with Passover, which is a spring feast with a different meaning.
Thinking tabernacle means only a church building; in this name it means a temporary dwelling.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name is chag ha-sukkot, the festival of booths, and the central word is sukkot, booths or huts. Leviticus 23:33-43 commands the seven-day feast and the living in booths to remember the wilderness journey. Deuteronomy 16:13-15 calls for joyful rejoicing at this harvest feast. John 7:2 mentions the feast as it approaches in Jerusalem, and Zechariah 14:16 looks ahead to nations keeping it.

senses.definition: A neural network in which the outputs are not used as input in a previous layer.

core.definition: A neural network in which information moves in one direction, from input layers through hidden layers to the output, with no loops back to earlier layers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FEED in the compound and NOO in 'neural', with NET in 'network'. The middle 'ward' is reduced to 'werd', and the 'r' in 'network' is clear in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It names a standard architecture and carries no evaluative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers in the US use this term constantly, often shortened to feedforward network or FNN, and it is standard in courses and papers. It contrasts with recurrent neural networks, which feed outputs back into the network. Say it as a noun phrase with the first element stressed.

distinctions.note: A recurrent network has loops that carry earlier outputs back as inputs, so it handles sequences with memory; a feedforward network has no such loops.
A convolutional network uses filters over local regions, mainly for images, while a feedforward network typically uses fully connected layers.

collocations: hidden layer in a feedforward network

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI said the simplest model we could try is a basic feedforward neural network.
examples.professional: Let's start with a feedforward neural network as the baseline before we try the transformer model.
examples.analytical: A feedforward neural network computes its output as a composition of layer transformations, with no state carried between inputs.

nuance.analogy: It is like an assembly line: parts move in one direction through each station, and no station sends a part back.
nuance.etymology: Feedforward combines feed and forward, from Old English fēdan and fore-weard; neural comes from Greek neuron (nerve); network from net and work.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'forward' as the main stress, when the compound stress falls on FEED.
Saying 'feed-forward' with a hyphen in formal writing; American technical writing usually closes it as one word.

senses.definition: To use or experience the sense of touch.
senses.example: You can feel a heartbeat if you put your fingers on your breast.

senses.definition: To become aware of through the skin; to use the sense of touch on.
senses.example: You can feel a heartbeat if you put your fingers on your breast.

senses.definition: To find one's way (literally or figuratively) by touching or using cautious movements.
senses.example: I felt my way through the darkened room.

senses.definition: To receive information by touch or by any neurons other than those responsible for sight, smell, taste, or hearing.
senses.example: I can feel the smooth stone under my fingers, cool and slightly wet.

senses.definition: To search by sense of touch.
senses.example: He felt (about) for the light switch in the dark.

senses.definition: To sense or think emotionally or judgmentally.
senses.example: I can feel the sadness in his poems.

senses.definition: To experience an emotion or other mental state about.
senses.example: I can feel the sadness in his poems.

senses.definition: To think, believe, or have an impression concerning.
senses.example: I feel that we need to try harder.

senses.definition: To experience an emotion or other mental state.
senses.example: He obviously feels strongly about it.

senses.definition: To sympathize; to have the sensibilities moved or affected.
senses.example: I feel for you and your plight.

senses.definition: To be or become aware of.
To experience the consequences of.
senses.example: Feel my wrath!

senses.definition: To seem (through touch or otherwise).
senses.example: It looks like wood, but it feels more like plastic.

senses.definition: To understand.
senses.example: I don't want you back here, ya feel me?

senses.definition: A perception experienced mainly or solely through the sense of touch.
senses.example: Bark has a rough feel.

senses.definition: A vague mental impression.
senses.example: You should get a feel for the area before moving in.

senses.definition: An act of fondling.
senses.example: She gave me a quick feel to show that she loves me.

senses.definition: A vague understanding.
senses.example: I'm getting a feel for what you mean.

senses.definition: An intuitive ability.
senses.example: She has a feel for music.

senses.definition: A feeling; an emotion.
senses.example: I know that feel.

core.definition: To experience a physical sensation through touch, or to be aware of an emotional or physical state, such as feeling tired or happy.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the vowel long and tense, like the 'ee' in 'see', not the short 'i' in 'fill'. The final 'l' is dark in American English, with the tongue pulled back.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is one of the most common verbs in English and carries no value judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use feel constantly for emotions and physical states: 'I feel great,' 'I feel sick,' 'I feel like we should talk.' In casual speech, people often answer 'How do you feel?' with 'Good' or 'Not great.' In formal writing, use feel for an emotion, but say 'I think' or 'I believe' for opinions.

distinctions.note: Touch names the physical contact itself, while feel names the sensation or awareness that results from it.
Feel describes your own experience or sensation; seem describes how something appears to you or to others.

examples.everyday: I feel a little tired, so I think I'm going to head home early tonight.
examples.professional: I feel the timeline is too tight, so let's talk about adding a week before we commit to the launch date.
examples.analytical: Kant holds that we feel the moral law as an obligation that binds us, rather than merely observing it as a fact about the world.

nuance.analogy: Feel is like a thermometer inside you: it registers what is happening in your body and mind so you can read it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fēlan (to touch, perceive by touch).
common_mistakes: Saying 'I feel bad' versus 'I feel badly': Americans say 'I feel bad' for an emotional or physical state, because 'badly' describes how you do something.
Saying 'I feel that' for an opinion in casual speech; the natural phrase is 'I feel like' or 'I think' for opinions.

feel.etymology: From Middle English *felen*, from Old English *fēlan*, from **fōlijan*.

senses.definition: To congratulate.

core.definition: To congratulate someone formally or warmly on an achievement or happy event.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LIS, and the final syllable rhymes with 'gate.' Do not pronounce the middle vowels as long E sounds; they are short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Positive and formal. It sounds ceremonial and a bit old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use felicitate mostly in formal letters, speeches, or official announcements. In everyday talk they say congratulate. Using felicitate with a friend would sound stiff or joking.

distinctions.note: Congratulate is the everyday word for all situations, while felicitate sounds formal and ceremonial.
Commend praises someone's qualities or conduct, while felicitate focuses on congratulating them for a happy event.

examples.everyday: I just wanted to felicitate you on the new baby, though I know it sounds a bit formal.
examples.professional: The board chair rose to felicitate the retiring director on thirty years of service.
examples.analytical: The essay opens by felicitating the author on a rare achievement, a formal courtesy that frames the critique to follow.

nuance.analogy: To felicitate someone is like handing them a formal certificate of congratulations rather than a casual high five.
nuance.etymology: From Latin felicitare, to make happy, from felix, happy.
common_mistakes: Using felicitate in casual conversation where congratulate is natural.
Confusing it with felicitous, which describes something apt or well chosen.

felicitate.etymology: From Latin *fēlicitātus*, perfect passive participle of *fēlīcitō* (“to felicitate”) (from *fēlīx* (“happy”)), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: To confess to something; to admit something.

core.definition: To admit a mistake, wrongdoing or secret, especially after being questioned or pressed. Usually followed by "to".

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle "up" most strongly, as with most phrasal verbs. "Fess" rhymes with "less," and the two words link smoothly, so "fess up" sounds like "fe-SUP" in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests the admission came after pressure or after being caught, not voluntarily.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this casually at home, at work, or with friends, often when someone finally admits breaking something or hiding something. It sounds playful, so it is not right for a formal apology or a legal statement. A natural reply is "Thanks for being honest" or "Okay, we figured."
word_family: fess (verb, informal short form of confess)

distinctions.note: Confess is more formal and serious and is used for crimes, sins or deep secrets. Fess up is casual and usually about everyday mistakes.
Own up to stresses taking responsibility for a mistake, often in a work or group setting. Fess up stresses the moment of admitting something that was hidden.

examples.everyday: Okay, fess up, who ate the last slice of pizza?
examples.professional: Before the retrospective, Dan finally fessed up to deleting the production logs by accident.
examples.analytical: The author argues that institutions rarely fess up to their failures until external pressure makes silence more costly than confession.

nuance.analogy: Like opening a drawer you have been keeping shut: the truth finally comes out in the open.
nuance.etymology: Fess is a shortened form of confess, from Latin confiteri, to acknowledge fully.
common_mistakes: Using "about" instead of "to" (say "fess up to it", not "fess up about it")
Writing "confess up" in casual contexts, which sounds unnatural
Using it in formal writing where "admit" or "acknowledge" is better

related: fess (verb, informal short form of confess)

senses.definition: Pertaining to or befitting a son or daughter.
senses.example: Her filial affection for her father showed in every letter she wrote from college.

senses.definition: Respectful of the duties and attitudes of sons or daughters toward their parents.
senses.example: His filial devotion meant he moved back home to care for his aging mother.

senses.definition: Of a generation or generations descending from a specific previous one.
senses.example: The first filial generation showed all dominant traits, as Mendel's experiments predicted.

core.definition: Relating to a son or daughter, especially showing the respect and duty that children owe their parents.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the final syllables to 'ee-uhl'. Many speakers say it nearly as 'FIL-yuhl', which is also acceptable.

nuance.connotation: Positive, implying respect and devotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say filial in casual talk; it appears in religious writing, academic discussion, and formal commentary on family duty. Phrases like 'filial piety' and 'filial duty' are the most common forms. In ordinary speech, people say 'dutiful' or 'respectful toward my parents'.

distinctions.note: Paternal refers to a father or fatherly behavior, while filial refers to the child's relation to a parent.
Dutiful is common and general; filial is formal and specifically about children's obligations to parents.

examples.everyday: She takes her filial duty seriously and calls her mother every Sunday.
examples.professional: In our family-leave policy, we recognize filial obligations such as caring for an aging parent.
examples.analytical: Confucian ethics treats filial piety as the foundation of social harmony.

nuance.analogy: Filial is the child's side of a family bond, as parental is the parent's side.
nuance.etymology: From Latin filialis, from filius (son) and filia (daughter).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'familial', which refers to family in general.
Pronouncing it as 'FIL-ee-al' with a long a at the end.

filial.etymology: From Middle English *filial*, from Latin *fīliālis*, from *fīlius* (“son”) / *fīlia* (“daughter”) + *-al*.

senses.definition: A basic, foundational proposition or assumption that cannot be deduced from any other proposition or assumption.

core.definition: A basic proposition or assumption that is not deduced from anything more basic and that other reasoning depends on.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PRIN in principle, and the second syllable of principle is reduced to a schwa, so the word ends in -pul, not -pal. Keep the flap sound out of the picture; the p and l are plain.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests clear, rigorous reasoning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in philosophy, science and engineering, and in business talk about reasoning from fundamentals. The plural 'first principles' is more common in everyday speech, as in 'let's reason from first principles.' Saying 'first principle' in the singular is typical in philosophy.

distinctions.note: An axiom is a starting statement within a formal system; a first principle is broader and can be philosophical or practical.
A premise is a statement used as a step in one particular argument; a first principle is a foundational assumption behind many arguments.

examples.everyday: My brother doesn't trust advice from anyone, so he likes to figure out how things work from first principles.
examples.professional: Let's reason from first principles about cost before we copy the vendor's pricing model.
examples.analytical: Descartes sought a first principle that could not be doubted, and from it he tried to derive the rest of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like the bedrock under a house: everything above it rests on it, and it rests on nothing else.
nuance.etymology: From Latin principium, 'beginning, foundation'.
common_mistakes: Using the singular where Americans say 'from first principles' in the plural
Confusing principle with principal, as in 'the principal idea'

senses.definition: To make something fixed and stable; to fix.
senses.example: Technicians used a special resin to fixate the fossil before moving it to the lab.

senses.definition: To stare fixedly at something.
senses.example: During the long sermon, Dad would fixate on the stained-glass window without blinking.

senses.definition: To attend to something to the exclusion of all others. [with on]
senses.example: Our team began to fixate on the minor bug and forgot the release deadline entirely.

senses.definition: To attach oneself to a person or thing in a pathological, neurotic, or obsessive manner. [with on]
senses.example: Some fans began to fixate on the actor's private life, obsessively tracking every appearance.

core.definition: To become obsessively focused on one thing, so that you cannot think about anything else. Usually used with on.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FIX. The final -ate is pronounced 'ayt,' not 'it,' and the t is a clear stop; many learners add a weak vowel or drop the t entirely.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative, suggesting obsession or a lack of balance, though it can be neutral when describing focus.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fixate on in everyday speech and in articles about psychology or media, for example 'Don't fixate on the mistake.' It can also mean to stare at something, but that sense is rare in everyday talk. Saying someone is fixated can sound critical, so be careful when describing a friend.

distinctions.note: Obsess is stronger and more emotional, often suggesting a constant, troubling preoccupation; fixate is more neutral and can describe a narrower focus of attention.
Focus is neutral and positive, describing deliberate attention; fixate suggests attention that has become rigid or excessive.

examples.everyday: Try not to fixate on the bad review; most of your customers are happy.
examples.professional: The project team fixated on the schedule and missed the real risk, which was the data quality.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard warns that the self can fixate on the finite and lose sight of its relation to the eternal.

nuance.analogy: Like a camera locked on one spot: it can capture a sharp image, but it misses everything else in the scene.
nuance.etymology: From the Latin fixus, 'fixed,' and the English verb ending -ate.
common_mistakes: Using fixate with 'of' or 'about' instead of 'on': the usual pattern is fixate on.
Confusing fixate with fix; fixate implies obsession, while fix means repair or make stable.

senses.definition: To burn brightly again.
senses.example: The fire flared up after we added more wood to it.

senses.definition: To become more intense suddenly.
senses.example: Reports indicate that tensions have flared up in the Middle East again.

senses.definition: To burst out suddenly, as in anger.
senses.example: The insult made him flare up.

core.definition: To suddenly become more intense, violent, or active, or to burst out in anger.

pronunciation.tip: 'Up' carries the stress in this phrasal verb. Link 'flare up' smoothly so it sounds like 'flair-UP'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes trouble or emotion breaking out unexpectedly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flare up' for conflicts, tempers, diseases, and pain, as in 'my back flared up.' In medical talk, a 'flare-up' is a sudden return of symptoms. A natural reply is 'Let's calm things down' or 'Is it getting better?'

distinctions.note: 'Explode' is more dramatic and often means a violent outburst; 'flare up' is usually shorter and may describe a sudden but temporary increase.
Erupt is more formal and suggests a powerful release; 'flare up' is everyday and can describe pain or illness.

examples.everyday: My knee flared up again after I hiked, so I'm icing it tonight.
examples.professional: The outage flared up during the release, so we rolled back the change.
examples.analytical: Old religious tensions flared up whenever the political settlement was questioned.

nuance.analogy: Like a match that suddenly burns bright before settling down, a problem flares up and then may die down.
nuance.etymology: 'Flare' (to blaze, possibly from Middle English) plus the adverb 'up'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'flare up' as one word in speech; it is two words, and the noun is 'flare-up'.
Using it for slow, gradual increases; it implies a sudden change.

conversation.text: My allergies flare up every spring.
His back pain flared up after he moved the couch.
My eczema flares up when the weather gets dry.

senses.definition: A design representing a flower whose three petals are joined together at the bottom (⚜, ⚜️), often used in heraldry, where it is particularly associated with the French monarchy.
senses.example: The gold fleur-de-lis on the shield identified the family as loyal to the French crown.

senses.definition: The main element in the logo of most Scouting organizations, representing a major theme in Scouting: the outdoors and wilderness.
senses.example: The troop's uniform patch showed a fleur-de-lis, the familiar Scouting emblem for outdoor adventure.

core.definition: A stylized symbol of a lily or iris with three joined petals, used in heraldry and as an emblem of French royalty and Scouting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable, 'LEE', and make the middle syllables reduced: 'flur-duh'. Americans usually say the final part as 'lee', not 'liss', though 'lis' is also heard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a decorative symbol with associations of royalty, heritage, and tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see the fleur-de-lis in New Orleans, on the New Orleans Saints logo, in Mardi Gras decorations, and in Boy Scouts emblems. The symbol is the emblem of the World Organization of the Scout Movement and of many national Scouting groups, not of all Scout organizations. It is a common word in design, travel, and local culture.

distinctions.note: An iris is the actual flower, while the fleur-de-lis is a stylized heraldic symbol based on it.
The trefoil is a three-leaf symbol used by Girl Scouts, while the fleur-de-lis has more elaborate curled petals.

examples.everyday: My friend has a fleur-de-lis on her front door as a little nod to New Orleans.
examples.professional: The design team placed a fleur-de-lis on the badge for the heritage brand because it signals tradition and quality.
examples.analytical: In medieval France, the fleur-de-lis functioned as a sign of royal legitimacy, linking the crown to a claim of divine favor.

nuance.analogy: A fleur-de-lis works like a logo that sticks: once you recognize it, every appearance of the symbol signals a particular heritage.
nuance.etymology: From French fleur, meaning flower, de, meaning of, and lis, meaning lily; literally 'flower of the lily'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'liss' when Americans usually say 'lee'.
Using 'fleur-de-lis' to mean a botanical iris or lily; it refers to the stylized symbol.

fleur-de-lis.etymology: From earlier *flower-de-luce* ("flower of light" by association with *lux*), from Middle English *flourdelis*, *flour delice*, from Anglo-Norman *flour de lis* (“lily flower”); the modern English form was remodelled after modern French *fleur de lis*…

senses.definition: A sandal consisting of a rubber sole fastened to the foot by a rubber thong fitting between the toes and around the sides of the foot.
senses.example: I packed my flip-flops for the beach trip, since we would be walking on sand all week.

senses.definition: A change of places; an inversion or swap.
senses.example: The team's sudden flip-flops in the lineup confused fans who had expected the starters to stay put.

senses.definition: An instance of flip-flopping, of repeatedly changing one's stated opinion about a matter.
senses.example: Voters were tired of the senator's endless flip-flops on the tax bill.
