senses.example: After ten years abroad, she agreed to pastor a small rural congregation in Ohio.

core.definition: The ordained minister who leads a Christian congregation, preaching, teaching, and caring for its members.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PASS. The final -or is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so say it like 'ter' without a strong t sound, almost a flap.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful. It names a church leader and is used warmly in congregations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use pastor for the leader of a Protestant church, and Catholics more often say priest or parish priest for the same role. People address a pastor as Pastor with the last name or as Pastor John in many churches. Calling a pastor by first name is common in some congregations, so follow local custom.

distinctions.note: A priest is a clergy member with sacramental authority, a term used especially in Catholic and Orthodox churches.
Minister is a broad term for any ordained church leader, often used in Protestant contexts.
A preacher is anyone who delivers sermons, while a pastor is the church's leader with ongoing care of its members.

examples.everyday: Our pastor is visiting the hospital this afternoon, so we can ask him about it then.
examples.professional: The pastor asked the staff to review the budget before the board meeting.
examples.analytical: In Ephesians the pastor is a gift to the church, equipping believers for their ministry and building up the body of Christ.

nuance.analogy: A pastor is like a shepherd who knows each sheep by name and walks with the flock through every season.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pastor, shepherd, from pascere, to feed.
common_mistakes: Using pastor for a Catholic priest in conversation without knowing the church tradition.
Stressing the second syllable, pa-STOR.
nuance.biblical_note: In Greek, poimen (ποιμήν) means shepherd, and in the New Testament it is used for church leaders. Ephesians 4:11 lists pastors and teachers among the gifts Christ gives to the church. In John 21:16 Jesus tells Peter to tend his sheep, and 1 Peter 5:2 urges elders to shepherd the flock of God.

traditions.view: Church leadership is exercised by bishops and priests, with the term pastor used more loosely and not as a formal office title.
The pastor is the priest canonically assigned to lead a parish with pastoral authority over its people and sacraments.
The pastor is an ordained minister who leads a congregation, though Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and Baptist churches differ on ordination and governance.

pastor.etymology: From Middle English *pastour*, from Old French *pastor* (Modern French *pasteur*), from Latin *pāstor*.

core.definition: In the Bible, Pathros is a region of Upper Egypt, the southern part of Egypt, where Jews lived and where the Lord promises to restore a remnant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the th is voiceless, as in "path." The final s is a clear s, not a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Pathros appears only in the Hebrew Bible and in Bible scholarship, so ordinary Americans rarely use it. Say it when discussing Jeremiah, Ezekiel or Isaiah, or the history of Judeans in Egypt. Use "Upper Egypt" or "southern Egypt" when explaining it to a general audience.
word_family: Pathrusim (noun, a people listed in Genesis 10:14)

distinctions.note: Egypt is the whole country, while Pathros names its southern region, the upper Nile valley.
Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt as a nation, while Pathros refers specifically to a southern territory.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group spent an hour on the prophets, and someone asked where Pathros is, so I told them it's southern Egypt.
examples.professional: In my lecture on Jeremiah, I pointed out that the Judeans who fled to Egypt settled in Pathros, not only in the Delta.
examples.analytical: Ezekiel's oracle that Egypt will return to Pathros, the land of its origin, frames the nation's restoration around its southern homeland.

nuance.analogy: Pathros is like a regional name such as "the Deep South" within a larger country: it points to a part of the whole.
nuance.etymology: From Egyptian p3-t3-rsy, meaning "the southern land."
common_mistakes: Saying it as "PATH-ross" with a hard th, or stressing the second syllable.
Treating Pathros as a city rather than a region.
nuance.biblical_note: Pathros is the Hebrew name Paṯrōs, from the Egyptian "the southern land," for Upper Egypt. Isaiah 11:11 lists Pathros among the lands from which the Lord will gather his remnant. Jeremiah 44:1 and 44:15 describe Judeans living in Pathros who were rebuked for worshiping other gods. Ezekiel 29:14 promises that Egypt will be restored to Pathros, the land of its origin, showing that even its exile is limited.

senses.definition: One who pays; specifically, the person by whom a bill or note has been, or should be, paid.
senses.example: The company is the largest tax payer in the region.

senses.definition: A swaption which gives its holder the option to enter into a swap in which they pay the fixed leg and receive the floating leg.
senses.example: The bank bought a payer swaption to hedge against rising interest rates next year.

core.definition: The person or organization that pays money owed, such as the party paying a bill, a loan, or an insurance claim.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PAY. The final syllable is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so it sounds like PAY-er, not PAY-air. Keep it distinct from player, which sounds the same only to careless ears.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term used in finance, healthcare, and contracts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use payer most often in healthcare and insurance, where a primary payer or third-party payer is the organization covering a bill. In everyday talk, people ask who's paying instead. In finance, payer also names the holder of a swap who pays the fixed side, which is a technical sense.

distinctions.note: The payer sends the money, while the payee receives it.
A customer buys goods or services, but the payer may be a third party such as an insurer.
A buyer agrees to purchase something, while the payer is the party who settles the bill.

examples.everyday: My insurance is the main payer, so I only owe the copay at the doctor's office.
examples.professional: We need to confirm which payer covers the claim before we schedule the procedure.
examples.analytical: In contract law, the identity of the payer matters when the obligation depends on another party's performance.

nuance.analogy: The payer is the one whose wallet actually opens when the bill comes due.
nuance.etymology: From pay plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who pays.
common_mistakes: Confusing payer with payee and saying the payer receives the money.
Pronouncing it as PLAY-er or PAY-air instead of PAY-er.

senses.definition: Without determination by or involvement of extraneous factors; by its very nature.
senses.example: Some people say that a hangover is caused by impurities in the drink, not by the alcohol per se.

senses.definition: As the principle of its own determination and positing itself.
senses.example: Hegel's logic presents the absolute as positing itself per se, determining its own ground.

senses.definition: Not leaving discretion to the judge to take into account additional factors that could rebut the judgment, deriving the qualification from the statute.
senses.example: The law makes drunk driving illegal per se.

senses.definition: Positing itself and being a principle of its own determination.
senses.example: Her essay treats freedom as a per se principle, one that determines itself without external cause.

senses.definition: That does not leave discretion to the judge to take into account additional factors that could rebut the judgment, deriving the qualification from the statute.
senses.example: The statute makes the offense illegal per se, so the judge may not consider mitigating factors.

core.definition: By its very nature, considered in itself and not because of other factors; in a strict sense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second word, SAY, while 'per' is weak. The Latin 'se' sounds like 'say', not 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it signals a careful qualification, so it sounds precise and intellectual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'per se' mostly in academic, legal and analytical speech to limit a claim: 'It isn't illegal per se.' In casual conversation 'in itself' or 'by itself' sounds more natural. It usually follows the word it modifies, and it is not a loose synonym for 'literally' or 'in particular'.

distinctions.note: 'In itself' is plain and common; 'per se' is more formal and often used in legal or academic argument.
'Literally' means in fact or word for word; 'per se' means intrinsically, considered by its nature alone.

collocations: not a bad idea per se

examples.everyday: I don't dislike the new team per se, but the weekly meetings drag.
examples.professional: The latency isn't a bug per se; it's a tradeoff we chose for the cache.
examples.analytical: Pleasure is not per se good; its moral value depends on what it serves and whom it harms.

nuance.analogy: Like judging a knife by its blade alone, not by who is holding it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin per se, 'through itself' or 'by itself'.
common_mistakes: Placing it at the start of a casual sentence, where it sounds stiff; say 'in itself' instead.
Using it as a synonym for 'literally' or 'in particular', which changes the meaning.
Stressing 'per' rather than 'se' in speech.

per-se.etymology: from *per* (“by, through”) and *sē* (“itself, himself, herself, themselves”).

senses.definition: In a persevering manner; with perseverance.

core.definition: In a steady, determined way, continuing to work toward a goal despite difficulty or setbacks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VIHR. End with a clear 'lee' sound, and keep the middle syllables light and quick.

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring.
nuance.usage_note: Perseveringly is rare in American speech and sounds literary. Americans prefer persistently, steadily, or doggedly. Use it in essays, reviews, or formal writing where you want to stress steady endurance.

distinctions.note: Persistently is everyday and can describe unwanted repetition, as in persistently late. Perseveringly always praises steady effort toward a goal.
Steadily stresses an even pace. Perseveringly stresses continuing despite difficulty.
Doggedly suggests stubborn, tenacious effort, sometimes with a hint of rigidity. Perseveringly sounds more admiring.

examples.everyday: She trained perseveringly all summer, and she finally finished the half-marathon this fall.
examples.professional: He debugged the data pipeline perseveringly until the failures disappeared from the logs.
examples.analytical: The author perseveringly defends her central claim against every objection raised in the previous chapter.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiker who keeps climbing after every switchback, even when the trail looks endless.
nuance.etymology: Formed from persevering and the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin perseverare.
common_mistakes: Using perseveringly in casual speech where persistently is more natural.
Dropping the final -ly sound, which makes the adverb sound like an adjective.

senses.definition: To show courage, strength, toughness, or responsibility; a gender-neutral alternative to "man up".

core.definition: To show courage, toughness, or responsibility, especially by facing a hard situation; a gender-neutral alternative to 'man up'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'up' in this phrasal verb, and 'person' has a reduced second syllable. In fast speech, 'person up' sounds like 'PUR-sn-UP' with the final n linked to the vowel of 'up'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly positive when used to encourage someone, but it can sound like a lecture or a joke. It is much less common than 'man up' and is mostly used online or by people who want to avoid gendered language.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'person up' informally, often in online discussions or to tease a friend. It is not standard in formal writing, so use 'take responsibility' or 'face it' in professional settings. A natural reply might be 'Okay, I'll own it' or 'Fair enough'. Some people find it awkward, so use it with friends rather than with a boss.

distinctions.note: 'Man up' is far more common and is often criticized as gendered; 'person up' is a deliberate neutral substitute that is rarely heard in everyday speech.
'Step up' means to take on more responsibility; 'person up' stresses courage in facing something difficult or unpleasant.

examples.everyday: Come on, person up and tell your sister you broke her phone.
examples.professional: When the deadline slipped, she persons up in the meeting and takes ownership of the delay.
examples.analytical: The coinage 'person up' revises a gendered idiom, but its informal tone and limited uptake show that the substitution has not displaced 'man up' in common usage.

nuance.analogy: It is like taking off a coat in a crowded room: you show the courage to stand out and face what is there.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English on the model of 'man up' by replacing 'man' with 'person' for gender-neutral use.
common_mistakes: Using 'person up' in formal writing, where 'take responsibility' is more appropriate.
Stressing 'person' too strongly, so the phrase sounds like three equal words.

senses.definition: A person who consumes no animal flesh with the exception of fish or seafood.
senses.example: My sister became a pescatarian, so she eats salmon but no chicken or beef.

senses.definition: Of or relating to pescetarianism.
senses.example: pescetarian diet

core.definition: A person who eats fish and seafood but no other meat, following a diet that is mostly vegetarian with fish included.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TAIR, the third syllable, and the first syllable is 'pes' like 'pest' without the t. The rhotic r is pronounced clearly in American speech, and the final syllables are weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a dietary choice. It can sound fussy if people find it an unnecessary label, but it is generally accepted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pescatarian' in restaurants, at dinner parties, and on food-delivery apps, often as a simple statement such as 'I'm pescatarian.' A natural reply is 'No problem, we have a salmon option,' or 'Got it, I'll check the menu for you.' Many people use the variant spelling 'pescetarian,' which is also correct.

distinctions.note: A vegetarian does not eat fish or seafood, while a pescatarian includes fish and seafood in an otherwise vegetarian diet.
A flexitarian mostly eats plants but occasionally eats meat, while a pescatarian eats fish regularly but no other meat.
A vegan avoids all animal products, including fish, dairy, and eggs, so it is much stricter than pescatarian.

examples.everyday: I'm pescatarian, so is there a fish option on the menu that isn't fried?
examples.professional: Please note the dietary needs on the catering order, since two of our guests are pescatarian and the default sandwiches have ham.
examples.analytical: Pescatarianism sits between vegetarianism and omnivory, and its ethical logic depends on how one weighs the suffering of fish.

nuance.analogy: A vegetarian with a seafood pass: plants are the base, and fish is the one animal food allowed.
nuance.etymology: From Italian pesce, 'fish,' and 'vegetarian.'
common_mistakes: Calling a pescatarian a vegetarian, which may lead to serving fish to someone who expects no fish at all, or to the wrong assumption about seafood.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, as in 'PES-kuh-tair-ee-un,' rather than on TAIR.

senses.definition: A lover of wisdom.
senses.example: My grandmother called herself a philosopher, a lover of wisdom who read every book she could find.

senses.definition: A student of philosophy.
A scholar or expert engaged in or contributing to philosophical inquiry.
senses.example: The philosopher spent her career examining how we justify beliefs about morality.

core.definition: A person who studies philosophy or thinks deeply and systematically about big questions such as knowledge, ethics, truth and how to live.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAH, not on the first or last syllable. The final syllable is a reduced vowel with an American r, so say 'fer' with the r colored, not 'fee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses. Calling someone a philosopher can praise their thoughtfulness, though it can also sound mildly sarcastic when someone talks too much about abstract ideas.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the word for academic professionals, but also for thoughtful friends. Saying 'You're a philosopher' to someone who makes calm, reflective comments is a compliment. In casual talk, 'deep thinker' is a common alternative.

distinctions.note: A thinker is anyone who thinks carefully; a philosopher is someone who studies fundamental questions in a disciplined way.
A theologian studies God and religious doctrine usually from within faith, while a philosopher reasons about such questions without assuming revelation.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a real philosopher; he can talk about life over coffee for hours.
examples.professional: Our vice president of product is a philosopher at heart, so she asks why before she asks how.
examples.analytical: Kant is often called the most influential modern philosopher because he reshaped how we think about the limits of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: A philosopher is like a detective of big questions, following each clue about truth and meaning back to its root.
nuance.etymology: From Greek philosophos, 'lover of wisdom', from philos 'loving' and sophia 'wisdom'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable and saying 'fi-LOS-o-fer'.
Dropping the final r or pronouncing the last syllable as 'fee'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word philosophos ('lover of wisdom') appears in the New Testament only as a loanword for Greek thinkers. In Acts 17:18 Paul debates with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers in Athens. In Colossians 2:8 Paul warns believers against being taken captive by philosophy that is empty deceit and based on human tradition rather than Christ. In 1 Corinthians 1:20-25 Paul says God has made the wisdom of the world foolish, contrasting human reasoning with the message of the cross.

traditions.view: Philosophy is valued as a tool for clear thinking, but Orthodox theology is cautious about letting philosophical systems define doctrine. Tradition and the experience of the Church guide theological truth.
Faith and reason are seen as complementary. Thomas Aquinas integrated Aristotelian philosophy into theology, and philosophy is treated as a real path to natural truths.

Views vary. Many Reformed and Lutheran writers have been wary of philosophy as a foundation for theology, emphasizing Scripture, while others, including some Anglican and evangelical thinkers, use philosophy to defend and explain the faith.

philosopher.etymology: From Middle English *philosophre*, from Anglo-Norman or Middle French *philosophe*, from Latin *philosophus*, from Ancient Greek *φιλόσοφος* + *-er*.

senses.definition: Nature, as contrasted with law or custom.
senses.example: Ancient Greek writers often set physis against nomos, arguing that some traits are natural rather than conventional.

senses.definition: The epiphyseal plate, a hyaline cartilage plate in the metaphysis at each end of a long bone, found in children and adolescents.
senses.example: The radiologist noted that the physis in the child's femur had not yet fused.

core.definition: In Greek philosophy and Orthodox theology, the nature of a thing, especially the nature of Christ as divine or human.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the word has two short syllables. Americans sometimes say the first vowel as a long i, which is correct here, but they often add an extra syllable, so keep it to two.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise theological and philosophical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use physis mainly in academic theology, classics, or philosophy, often in discussions of Christology or Greek thought. It is not an everyday word. Most English speakers would say nature, and theologians often add the Greek word for emphasis or precision.

distinctions.note: Nature is the general English word. Physis is a technical Greek term that emphasizes the essential constitution of a thing.
Physis is the nature or essence, while hypostasis is the concrete person or subsistence that possesses that nature.

examples.everyday: At our church reading group, someone asked what the word physis means, and I said it's the Greek word for nature.
examples.professional: In the seminar, I'll explain why the council used physis when discussing the two natures of Christ.
examples.analytical: The Chalcedonian definition distinguishes physis from hypostasis, affirming two physeis in the one hypostasis of the incarnate Word.

nuance.analogy: Physis is like the blueprint built into a thing, the nature that determines what it is and what it can do.
nuance.etymology: From Greek phusis, nature, from the verb phuein, to grow or to bring forth.
common_mistakes: Using physis as a synonym for physics or physical.
Treating physis and hypostasis as the same thing in Christological discussions.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word physis, nature, appears in the New Testament, for example in Romans 2:14, where Gentiles do by nature what the law requires. Ephesians 2:3 says that by nature we were children of wrath, and Galatians 4:8 says that those who by nature are no gods were enslaved to them. Orthodox writers use the word extensively in Christology.

traditions.view: Christ has two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation in one hypostasis, as defined at Chalcedon. Physis is used to affirm that each nature retains its properties.
Christ is one divine person with two natures, divine and human, as affirmed at the Council of Chalcedon. The distinction of natures is upheld while the unity of the person is maintained.

Most Protestants accept the Chalcedonian two-natures formula. Lutherans stress the communication of attributes between the natures, while Reformed theologians emphasize that the finite human nature cannot contain the infinite divine nature.

senses.definition: Rogue, adventurer.

core.definition: A roguish, clever character who survives by his wits, especially the hero of a picaresque adventure story.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the middle vowel short and clean. Do not stress the last syllable as in 'pi-KAR-oh', and give the final r a light American sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive, suggesting a charming scoundrel who is more clever than wicked. It is almost always used in literary or critical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly meet this word in literature classes and discussions of Spanish novels such as Lazarillo de Tormes. In everyday conversation, say 'rogue', 'scoundrel' or 'charmer' instead. You will rarely hear it in casual talk, so use it in writing or analysis.
word_family: picaresque (noun, a genre of episodic rogue narratives)

distinctions.note: Rogue is common everyday English for a dishonest or mischievous person, while picaro is a literary term for a clever, low-born wanderer who lives by his wits.
Scoundrel is a stronger word for a bad person, while picaro suggests a likable, resourceful survivor.

examples.everyday: My cousin is kind of a picaro, always talking his way out of trouble and somehow ending up on top.
examples.professional: The screenplay's protagonist is a picaro whose schemes drive the plot from one city to the next.
examples.analytical: Lazarillo de Tormes established the picaro as a figure who narrates his own survival in a corrupt society.

nuance.analogy: A picaro is like a street-smart Huck Finn who keeps getting into trouble and always finds a way out.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish picaro, from picar 'to prick, sting', suggesting a sharp, cunning person.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as in 'pi-KAR-oh', when English puts the stress on the first syllable.
Using picaro for any criminal; it specifically implies a clever, often likable rogue in a story.

senses.definition: To notice, observe, learn, or understand, especially something otherwise overlooked.
To continue or build upon (for example, a task, analysis, or narrative), beginning from a point at which someone has previously stopped.
To adopt a practice in which others already engage.

core.definition: To notice a subtle hint, mood or detail that others might miss, often without being told.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on on in this phrasal verb, so say pik-up-AHN. In fast speech, up blends into on, so it sounds almost like 'pi-kup-PAHN'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing attentiveness, and neutral or negative when describing someone who notices tension or problems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this often for people or animals who sense things: 'Kids pick up on tension quickly.' It is about perceiving something, not learning a skill. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I picked up on that too.'

distinctions.note: Notice is general and neutral, while pick up on suggests noticing something subtle that was not obvious.
Pick up alone can mean lifting something, buying something or learning a skill; pick up on specifically means perceiving a hint or detail.

examples.everyday: My dog always picks up on it when I'm stressed.
examples.professional: Our new analyst picked up on a data gap that the whole team had missed.
examples.analytical: A careful reader picks up on the subtle shift in meaning between the two translations.

nuance.analogy: Picking up on something is like a smoke detector catching the first faint whiff of smoke.
common_mistakes: Placing it after on, as in 'pick up it on'; the correct form is 'pick up on it'.
Using pick up on to mean learning a skill; for learning, Americans say 'pick up' a new skill, like pick up Spanish.

senses.definition: Gerund of pierce.
A hole made in the body so that jewelry can be worn through it.
senses.example: ear piercing

senses.definition: An item of jewelry designed to be fitted through a piercing (noun sense 2).
senses.example: She chose a small gold piercing for her cartilage after months of thinking about it.

senses.definition: Appearing to look deeply into; penetrating.
senses.example: piercing eyes

senses.definition: Of temperature, extremely cold so that it penetrates through clothing and shelter.
Of sound, loud and sharp; shrill.
senses.example: The piercing noise of the children could be heard two blocks from the elementary school.

core.definition: Sharp and penetrating, such as a look that seems to see through you, a loud high sound, or bitter cold that gets through your clothes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the vowel short, as in 'pir', not 'peer'. The r is clearly pronounced, and the -ing ending is a light nasal sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative: a piercing look or sound can be admiring or uncomfortable, depending on context and tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for eyes, screams, winds and cold, as in 'piercing blue eyes' or 'a piercing wind.' As a noun, it also refers to body jewelry, so 'I want a nose piercing' is natural. Describing a person's gaze as piercing can be a compliment or a sign of discomfort.

distinctions.note: Sharp is a general word for quick, keen or cutting; piercing specifically suggests something that penetrates deeply.
Shrill describes a high, harsh voice or sound, while piercing can also describe a look or cold.
Penetrating is more formal and often used for insight or analysis; piercing suggests a sharper, more physical or emotional impact.

examples.everyday: The baby let out a piercing scream right in the middle of the grocery store.
examples.professional: Her piercing questions in the design review found a bug that nobody else had noticed.
examples.analytical: The author's piercing critique of institutional religion exposes the gap between creed and everyday conduct.

nuance.analogy: A piercing sound is like a needle through cloth: thin, sharp and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From pierce, from Middle English percen, plus the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'peircing', which breaks the rule that i comes before e; pierce is an exception.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'pir-SING'; the stress falls on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrews 4:12 the word of God is described as 'piercing' (Greek diïknoumenos, penetrating through), sharper than any two-edged sword and able to divide soul and spirit. Luke 2:35 says that a sword will pierce through Mary's own soul, a prophecy of grief that the RSV expresses with the verb 'pierce' rather than the adjective.

senses.definition: Having pillars.
senses.example: We entered a majestic pillared hall.

core.definition: Having or supported by pillars, such as a building with a row of columns across its front.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the final 'ed' as a 'd' sound after the r, so it sounds like 'PIL-erd,' with no extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes architecture or design and has no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pillared mainly to describe buildings, porches, or rooms, such as a pillared portico or a pillared hall. It is common in real estate, architecture, and travel descriptions, and it sounds slightly elegant. In casual talk, people usually say 'with columns' for a house or building.

distinctions.note: Columned and pillared have nearly the same meaning, but columned is more common in American architectural writing, while pillared sounds more literary.
Colonnaded means having a row or walkway lined with columns, while pillared can describe any structure supported by pillars.
Pillar is a noun for the support itself, while pillared is an adjective describing something that has pillars.

examples.everyday: We drove past a big white house with a pillared porch, and my wife said she wanted one just like it.
examples.professional: The architect's proposal includes a pillared lobby that will make the entrance more welcoming for visitors.
examples.analytical: The pillared façade of the courthouse was designed to suggest the stability and authority of the republic.

nuance.analogy: Pillared is like a tree trunk: the columns hold up the weight of the roof, just as trunks support a canopy.
nuance.etymology: From pillar, with the -ed suffix forming an adjective meaning having pillars.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final 'ed' as a separate syllable, as in 'PIL-er-ed.'
Using pillared for a single column, when it means having several pillars.
Confusing pillared with pillowed, which describes something soft and cushioned.

senses.definition: The use of landmarks to guide a vessel or aircraft to its destination.
senses.example: Before modern GPS, sailors relied on pilotage, navigating by church spires and headlands.

senses.definition: The occupation of a pilot.
senses.example: He left the navy and took up pilotage on the Chesapeake Bay.

senses.definition: The fee paid to a pilot who guides a ship to its anchorage (a roadstead or wharf) or to its outbound channel.
senses.example: The harbor authority billed the freighter for pilotage, anchorage, and port fees.

core.definition: The act of navigating a ship or aircraft by using visible landmarks, or the job of guiding ships through difficult waters, such as harbors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PY. The middle 'ot' reduces to a weak 'luh', and the ending '-age' sounds like 'ij', as in 'courage'. Do not stress the ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used in maritime and aviation contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pilotage' mostly in maritime and aviation settings, such as harbor pilots, port authorities, and navigation training. In everyday boating talk, people usually say 'piloting' or 'navigation'. The term appears in official fees, regulations, and training manuals.

distinctions.note: Pilotage is a specific kind of navigation based on landmarks and local knowledge. Piloting is the broader activity of steering and navigating a vehicle.
Dead reckoning calculates position from speed, heading, and elapsed time without visual references. Pilotage relies on what you can see around you.

examples.everyday: My uncle used to talk about pilotage in the harbor, and I never quite understood what he meant.
examples.professional: The harbor authority charges a pilotage fee for every inbound container ship that needs a local guide.
examples.analytical: Pilotage depends on visible landmarks, so its accuracy declines in fog, which is why instruments became essential.

nuance.analogy: Pilotage is like following familiar road signs while driving. Dead reckoning is like driving with your eyes closed, using only your speed and time.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'pilot' plus the suffix '-age', which indicates a function or charge.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'pi-lo-TAGE'.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'lo' with a long o, when it should be a weak 'luh'.
Confusing 'pilotage' with 'piloting' in general conversation, where 'piloting' is more common.

senses.definition: An undesirable pink-colored microbial mass occurring in the slurry used in making paper.
senses.example: The mill manager found pink slime clinging to the pipes in the paper-making slurry.

senses.definition: A meat byproduct produced from scraps by heating and then treating with ammonia to produce a food additive.
Low-quality, mass-produced internet content, especially AI-generated.
senses.example: Half the search results were pink slime, churned out by bots with no real author.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see pink,‎ slime. Slime which is pink.
senses.example: The kids giggled over the bowl of pink slime they had made from glue and food coloring.

core.definition: A pink, processed beef product made from fatty scraps, treated with ammonia and used in ground meat.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on slime, the second word, and pink takes a lighter secondary stress. Keep the ng in pink clean and let the l in slime stay light.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests something unappealing and artificially made, so it is often used to criticize food or content.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use pink slime to refer to the processed beef product that became a national news topic in the late 2000s. Because it is a loaded term, it is common in news, food debates and online commentary. It is also used figuratively for low-quality content, but in casual conversation the food meaning is the main one.

distinctions.note: Ground beef is the general product name, while pink slime is a specific, critical term for a particular processed beef additive.
Filler is a neutral word for cheap added material, while pink slime is a stronger, more negative word.

examples.everyday: Did you hear about pink slime being added to hamburger meat, or is that just a rumor?
examples.professional: The sourcing team asked the supplier to confirm that no pink slime was used in the beef blend.
examples.analytical: The term pink slime was a rhetorical choice that turned a technical food additive into a moral scandal about what people eat.

nuance.analogy: Pink slime is like a cheap filler in a sandwich that the maker hopes you won't notice until you take a bite.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 2000s by a U.S. Department of Agriculture microbiologist, Gerald Zirnstein, as a description for lean finely textured beef.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as pink SLIME with equal stress on both words, which sounds unnatural.
Assuming it refers to a color or a children's toy rather than the food product.

senses.definition: In AI: A sequence of steps that data or a model goes through, such as cleaning, training, evaluation and deployment.
A conduit made of pipes used to convey water, gas or petroleum, etc.
senses.example: An oil pipeline has been opened from the Caspian Sea.

senses.definition: A channel (either physical or logical) by which information is transmitted sequentially (that is, the first information in is the first information out).
senses.example: 3D images are rendered using the graphics pipeline.

senses.definition: A system or process through which something is conducted.
senses.example: A new version of the software is in the pipeline, but has not been rolled out.

senses.definition: A widely observed pattern of development in personal interests, circumstances, or opinions.
senses.example: Many who grew up in foster homes in the county have fallen victim to the foster-care-to-homelessness pipeline.

senses.definition: A continuous, contributing source of benefits, talent, or innovation.
senses.example: Our university has been a steady pipeline of talented engineers for Silicon Valley firms.

senses.definition: The inside of a wave that a surfer is riding, when the wave has started closing over it.
senses.example: The surfer tucked deep inside the pipeline as the wave curled over his head.

senses.definition: To design (a microchip etc.) so that processing takes place in efficient stages, the output of each stage being fed as input to the next.
senses.example: Engineers decided to pipeline the processor so each instruction moves through several stages.

senses.definition: To convey by a system of pipes.
senses.example: The utility company will pipeline natural gas from the Texas fields to the coast.

senses.definition: To lay a system of pipes through.
senses.example: Crews plan to pipeline the desert region before the summer construction season begins.

core.definition: A long pipe that carries oil, gas or water over a distance, or a series of stages things pass through (a sales pipeline); in AI and data science, a sequence of automated steps, such as cleaning data, training a model and deploying it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PIPE, and make the second syllable a lighter, quick line. Do not add an extra vowel between the two parts, and keep the final n clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a process or structure. In business it can describe a sales pipeline, which is positive when it is full and healthy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pipeline very widely in tech, data teams, and business meetings. In data science, people say the training pipeline or the data pipeline. In sales, a full pipeline means many potential deals, and a sales meeting may ask how the pipeline looks. Outside work, the word sounds a bit technical, so people might say process or workflow instead.

distinctions.note: Workflow is a broader term for any sequence of human or automated tasks, while pipeline usually implies a more automated, data-driven flow of stages.
Process is a general word for any series of steps, while pipeline emphasizes a chain in which the output of one stage becomes the input of the next.

examples.everyday: Our sales pipeline looks really strong this month, so I think we will hit the target.
examples.professional: I rebuilt the training pipeline so the model retrains automatically whenever new data arrives.
examples.analytical: A machine learning pipeline makes each transformation explicit, which improves reproducibility and makes errors easier to trace.

nuance.analogy: Like a factory assembly line, each stage hands its finished work to the next, so raw data comes out as a finished product.
nuance.etymology: From pipe plus line, from the physical pipe network used to carry liquids, later applied to a sequence of processing stages.
common_mistakes: Saying pipe line as two words in technical writing, when the standard form is pipeline.
Using pipeline only for physical pipes, and missing the common AI and sales meanings.

conversation.text: The training pipeline pulls data, cleans it, trains, evaluates, and registers the model.
Our RAG pipeline has three stages: retrieve, rerank, and generate.
Pipeline parallelism splits the model's layers across GPUs in sequential stages.
The sales pipeline looks strong for next quarter.

senses.definition: A sticky, gummy substance secreted by trees; tree sap.
senses.example: It is hard to get this pitch off my hand.

senses.definition: Anything similar to or derived from tree sap: resin; rosin.
senses.example: The old pine floorboards were coated with sticky amber pitch that never fully dried.

senses.definition: A dark, extremely viscous material still remaining after distilling crude oil or natural tar.
senses.example: They put pitch on the mast to protect it.

senses.definition: A throw; a toss; a cast, as of something from the hand.
senses.example: a good pitch in quoits

senses.definition: A short, high, lofty shot that lands with backspin.
senses.example: She hit a high pitch over the bunker that landed softly and spun back toward the flag.

senses.definition: An effort to sell or promote something.
senses.example: He gave me a sales pitch.

senses.definition: The distance between evenly spaced objects, e.g. the teeth of a saw or gear, the turns of a screw thread, the centers of holes, or letters in a monospace font.
senses.example: The pitch of pixels on the point scale is 72 pixels per inch.

senses.definition: The angle at which an object sits.
senses.example: the pitch of the roof or haystack

senses.definition: The rotation angle about the transverse axis.
senses.example: the pitch of an aircraft

senses.definition: A measure of the angle of attack of a propeller.
senses.example: The propeller blades' pitch went to 90° as the engine was feathered.

senses.definition: An area in a market (or similar) allocated to a particular trader.
senses.example: Our family has rented the same farmers market pitch for twelve years running.

senses.definition: The place where a busker performs, a prostitute solicits clients, or an illegal gambling game etc. is set up before the public.
senses.example: The street musician moved his pitch closer to the subway exit after the police told him to leave.

senses.definition: An area on a campsite intended for occupation by a single tent, caravan or similar.
senses.example: Our campground assigned us a shady pitch near the lake for the weekend.

senses.definition: A level or degree, or, a peak or highest degree.
senses.example: Tension in the negotiations reached a pitch when the union walked out of the room.

senses.definition: A point or peak; the extreme point of elevation or depression.
senses.example: The hikers finally reached the pitch of the ridge just before the storm arrived.

senses.definition: The most thrust-out point of a headland or cape.
senses.example: The lighthouse stands on the rocky pitch of the cape, facing the open Atlantic.

senses.definition: The height a bird reaches in flight, especially a bird of prey preparing to swoop down on its prey.
senses.example: The hawk hung motionless at a great pitch above the field before diving at the mouse.

senses.definition: Prominence; importance.
senses.example: The senator gave the issue great pitch in her campaign speeches.

senses.definition: A section of a climb or rock face; specifically, the climbing distance between belays or stances.
senses.example: The third pitch of the route was the hardest, with a long crack and few holds.

senses.definition: A vertical cave passage, only negotiable by using rope or ladders.
senses.example: The entrance pitch requires 30 meters of rope.

senses.definition: A descent; a fall; a thrusting down.
senses.example: The plane's sudden pitch downward terrified the passengers in the back rows.

senses.definition: The point where a declivity begins; hence, the declivity itself; a descending slope; the degree or rate of descent or slope; slant.
senses.example: a steep pitch in the road

senses.definition: The limit of ground set to a miner who receives a share of the ore taken out.
senses.example: Under the old mining charter, each prospector received a pitch of ground along the creek.

senses.definition: An American trick-taking card game.
senses.example: On Friday nights, the retirees at the community center play pitch until late.

senses.definition: Pitchstone.
senses.example: The geology professor placed a dark piece of pitch on the desk and asked us to describe it.

senses.definition: The act of pitching a baseball.
senses.example: The pitch was low and inside.

senses.definition: The degree to which a vehicle, especially a ship or aircraft, rotates on such an axis, tilting its bow or nose up or down.
senses.example: the pitch of an aircraft

senses.definition: That point of the ground on which the ball pitches or lights when bowled.
senses.example: The ball struck a damp spot on the pitch and swung sharply toward the slips.

senses.definition: The perceived frequency of a sound, note or electromagnetic wave.
senses.example: The pitch of middle "C" is familiar to many musicians.

senses.definition: The standard to which a group of musical instruments are tuned or in which a piece is performed, usually by reference to the frequency to which the musical note A above middle C is tuned.
senses.example: Are we in baroque pitch for this one?

senses.definition: In an a cappella group, the singer responsible for singing a note for the other members to tune themselves by.
senses.example: Bob, our pitch, let out a clear middle "C" and our conductor gave the signal to start.

senses.definition: (rare) The field of battle.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To cover or smear with pitch.
To darken; to blacken; to obscure.
To throw.
senses.example: He pitched the horseshoe.

senses.definition: To throw away; discard.
senses.example: He pitched the candy wrapper.

senses.definition: To promote, advertise, or attempt to sell.
senses.example: He pitched the idea for months with no takers.

senses.definition: To deliver in a certain tone or style, or with a certain audience in mind.
senses.example: At which level should I pitch my presentation?

senses.definition: To assemble or erect (a tent). Also used figuratively.
senses.example: Pitch the tent over there.

senses.definition: To fix or place a tent or temporary habitation; to encamp.
To set at an angle, especially a downwards one; to cause to tilt.
To play a short, high, lofty shot that lands with backspin.
senses.example: The only way to get on the green from here is to pitch the ball over the bunker.

senses.definition: To settle and build up, without melting.
To fix one's choice.
To plunge or fall; especially, to fall forward; to decline or slope.
senses.example: to pitch from a precipice

senses.definition: To set, face, or pave (an embankment or roadway) with rubble or undressed stones.
To set or fix (a price or value).
To discard (a card) for some gain.
To attack, or position or assemble for attack.
To add yeast as a step while making beer.
To produce a note of a given pitch.
To fix or set the tone of.
To throw (the ball) toward a batter at home plate.
senses.example: The hurler pitched a curveball.

senses.definition: To play baseball in the position of pitcher.
senses.example: Bob pitches today.

senses.definition: To move so that the front of an aircraft or boat goes alternately up and down.
senses.example: The typhoon pitched the deck of the ship.

senses.definition: To bounce on the playing surface.
senses.example: The ball pitched well short of the batsman.

senses.definition: Very dark black; pitch-black.
Intense, deep, dark.

core.definition: To throw a ball toward a batter in baseball, or to present an idea or product to someone, trying to win their support.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short i, as in 'sit', followed by the 'ch' sound. Do not lengthen the vowel to 'peach', which is a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes a normal throw or presentation, though 'sales pitch' can suggest a sales push.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pitch' often in baseball and in business. You can pitch a product, an idea or a project to a boss or investors. In startup culture, 'pitch deck' and 'elevator pitch' are common. A natural reply to 'Let me pitch you an idea' is 'Sure, go ahead.'

distinctions.note: Present is more formal and neutral, while 'pitch' implies you are trying to persuade or sell.
Throw is general, while 'pitch' in baseball means an underhand or overhand throw aimed at a batter.

examples.everyday: My brother is trying to pitch me on buying a used boat.
examples.professional: Maya will pitch the new dashboard to the product team on Thursday.
examples.analytical: Pitching a theory requires not only evidence but also a sense of what the audience already believes.

nuance.analogy: Like throwing a ball toward a catcher's mitt: you aim your idea so the listener can catch it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English picchen, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'peach' with a long vowel.
Confusing 'pitch' with 'pick' or 'patch'.
Saying 'pitch me the idea' in formal writing; use 'present' or 'share' if you want a neutral tone.
nuance.biblical_note: In Genesis 6:14, Noah is told to cover the ark inside and out with pitch, translated from the Hebrew kopher, meaning pitch or bitumen. Exodus 2:3 says the basket for the infant Moses was daubed with bitumen and pitch to make it watertight.

pitch.etymology: From Middle English *picche*, *piche*, *pich*, from Old English *piċ*, from **pik*, from Latin *pix*.

senses.definition: In a pitiless manner.

core.definition: In a cruel and merciless way, showing no sympathy for someone's suffering or distress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the middle syllables short and reduced. The final -ly is a clear 'lee', and the -less- is a quick 'luss'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes harshness, cruelty, or a lack of sympathy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pitilessly in formal writing, news, and serious description of cruelty or indifference. In casual talk they more often say mercilessly or harshly. It can describe weather, nature, or a critic as easily as a person. It is strong, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Mercilessly means without mercy or without sparing someone; pitilessly stresses the lack of sympathy for suffering.
Ruthlessly often describes calculated pursuit of goals, while pitilessly focuses on the absence of compassion.

examples.everyday: The sun beat down pitilessly on the hikers all afternoon, and nobody had brought enough water.
examples.professional: The auditors examined the spreadsheets pitilessly and flagged every inconsistency we had missed.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky's narrator examines his own motives pitilessly, refusing any comfortable excuse.

nuance.analogy: Pitilessly is like a winter storm that does not slow down for anyone, no matter how cold or tired they are.
nuance.etymology: From pitiless (from pity plus -less) and the adverbial ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using pitilessly for a neutral or merely strict action, where a milder word like strictly is better.
Confusing it with pitifully, which expresses pity rather than the lack of it.
Pronouncing the middle syllables too clearly, as in 'PIT-ih-luss-LESS-lee'.

senses.definition: In a plain manner; simply; basically.
senses.example: She decorated the room plainly but neatly.

senses.definition: Obviously; clearly.
senses.example: You will see that ours is plainly the better method.

core.definition: In a clear, direct way that is easy to understand, without decoration or hidden meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PLAYN. The final -ly is a short 'lee' sound, and there is no extra vowel between the n and the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals honesty and directness, though it can sound blunt or stern if used to correct someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'plainly' to introduce a direct statement, as in 'Plainly, we need more time.' In casual talk, 'to put it plainly' is common. 'Obviously' and 'clearly' are the usual alternatives when you mean something is evident.

distinctions.note: Simply focuses on ease or basics, while plainly focuses on open, direct expression or on what is obvious.
Clearly describes how easy something is to see or understand; plainly often adds a note of frankness.

examples.everyday: To put it plainly, the restaurant is closed on Mondays.
examples.professional: Plainly, the forecast missed because our churn assumptions were too optimistic.
examples.analytical: The author states plainly that grace precedes works, and this shapes the rest of the argument.

nuance.analogy: Plainly is like a window with no curtains: you can see straight through.
nuance.etymology: From plain, from Old French plain, 'flat, clear', from Latin planus, 'flat', plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using plainly where you need the adjective plain, as in 'It tastes plain' rather than 'plainly'.
Confusing plain, meaning simple, with plain meaning unattractive.
Pronouncing the ending as 'lie' instead of 'lee'.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV 'plainly' in John 16:25 translates Greek parrēsia (παρρησία), openness or frankness of speech. In John 16:25 Jesus says he will no longer speak in figures but will tell of the Father openly, and in John 10:24 the Jews ask him to tell them plainly whether he is the Christ. Habakkuk 2:2 tells the prophet to write the vision and make it plain, from Hebrew bā'ar (בָּאַר), to make clear.

senses.definition: An abundant supply; abundance.

core.definition: The state of being abundant; a large, generous supply or amount of something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PLEN. The -teous part is 'tee-us' and the final -ness is a reduced 'nus', not a long 'nes'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it suggests generosity and blessing, but it sounds old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Almost nobody says plenteousness in modern American speech. You may meet it in older hymns, sermons or literary works. Americans say abundance, plenty or a large supply. In most formal writing, abundance is the better choice.

distinctions.note: Abundance is the standard American word for a large amount and is common in speech and writing; plenteousness is archaic or literary.
Plenty is everyday and informal, as in there's plenty of food; plenteousness is more elevated and often used for harvests or blessings.

examples.everyday: My grandfather talked about the plenteousness of the harvest every fall, and we never got tired of hearing it.
examples.professional: The report's plenteousness of data impressed the board, but the team still needs clearer conclusions.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of grace stresses the plenteousness of God's gift, which exceeds any merit humans can earn.

nuance.analogy: Plenteousness is like a river in flood season: more water than the banks seem able to hold.
nuance.etymology: From plenteous (Old French plentif, from Latin plenus 'full') plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using it in ordinary talk instead of abundance or plenty.
Confusing it with plentifulness, which is the more common modern noun.

senses.definition: In a plucky manner.

core.definition: In a brave, spirited way, especially while facing difficulty, hardship or a bad situation without giving up.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and use a short 'u' as in 'cup'. The final '-ly' is a light 'lee', and the 'ck' is a single hard 'k' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises courage and determination, often in journalism or storytelling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'pluckily' in casual talk. It appears more often in news stories, book reviews and literary writing. In everyday speech you would say 'bravely', 'gamely' or 'with a lot of guts'. Use it when you want a polished, slightly old-fashioned tone.

distinctions.note: Bravely is the everyday word for courage, while pluckily adds a sense of spirited determination in a small or difficult situation.
Gamely means willingly and cheerfully taking on a difficult challenge, often in sports or games, which is narrower than pluckily.

examples.everyday: He pluckily kept fixing the fence, even though the storm kept knocking it down.
examples.professional: The team pluckily kept pushing the launch date forward despite losing two engineers.
examples.analytical: The novel's heroine acts pluckily, not from confidence but from a stubborn refusal to be defeated by her circumstances.

nuance.analogy: Pluckily is like a seedling pushing up through a crack in the sidewalk: small, but stubbornly determined to grow anyway.
nuance.etymology: From plucky, from pluck (courage), which comes from the Old English pluccian meaning to pull or pluck.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'pluckily' with 'luckily', which means by good fortune.
Using 'pluckily' in casual speech, where 'bravely' or 'gamely' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: One who plunders or pillages.
senses.example: The plunderer rode through the village at dawn, taking grain, livestock, and silver from every house.

core.definition: A person who steals goods by force, especially during war, riot, or disaster, or who takes property from a place by violence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PLUN, and the middle syllable is weak, like 'der' in 'other.' The final -er is reduced and not a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use plunderer mainly in history, literature, and formal writing about war or conquest. In everyday speech, people usually say looter after a storm or riot, or thief for ordinary theft. The word suggests violence and a large scale of taking.

distinctions.note: Looter is the usual American term for someone who steals during a disaster or riot, while plunderer is more formal and historical.
A pirate attacks ships at sea, while a plunderer can attack towns, cities, or lands.
A raider makes a quick attack to seize things, while a plunderer focuses on the taking of goods.

examples.everyday: The old movie showed a gang of plunderers riding into the village at dawn.
examples.professional: Our insurance team calls people who steal from damaged properties after storms plunderers, though police usually say looters.
examples.analytical: Historians often describe the Norse plunderers as merchants who used violence to open trade routes, not just as mindless raiders.

nuance.analogy: Like a flood that sweeps through a town and carries away everything it can reach, a plunderer leaves a place stripped bare.
nuance.etymology: From plunder plus -er; plunder comes from a German word meaning to plunder.
common_mistakes: Using plunderer for ordinary shoplifting, where thief is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable, as in plun-DER-er.

senses.definition: A politician.

core.definition: An informal short form of politician, used in news and casual talk about people in public office.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the dark cot vowel, so it rhymes with 'pod' plus an l sound. Do not say it like 'pole' or 'Paul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly dismissive, depending on tone. It is casual and can sound flippant in serious writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'pol' mainly in headlines, social media and casual talk, as in 'a local pol' or 'an old-school pol'. In formal writing, say 'politician'. Calling someone a pol can sound dismissive, so choose it with care.

distinctions.note: 'Politician' is the standard word for anyone who seeks or holds political office, while 'pol' is a clipped, informal form that can sound a little dismissive.

examples.everyday: My uncle knows every local pol in town, so he always hears the gossip first.
examples.professional: Our communications team wants a quote from a pol who supported the bill, not just another press release.
examples.analytical: Readers who rely on pol soundbites often miss the policy details buried in the committee report.

nuance.etymology: Shortened from politician, which traces back to Greek politēs, citizen.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an oh vowel like 'pole'; in General American it has the short cot vowel.
Using 'pol' in formal writing, where 'politician' is expected.

senses.definition: Made unclean or impure.

core.definition: Made dirty or impure by harmful substances, such as polluted air, water or soil.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LOO, and the ending '-ed' is pronounced 'id', so the word has three syllables. Say the u as 'oo', not 'yoo'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something harmful or unsafe, not just dirty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use polluted for water, air, rivers and land with harmful contamination, often in news and warnings, as in 'Don't swim here, the water is polluted.' In casual talk, 'dirty' is more common for ordinary grime. In figurative speech, people sometimes say a debate or culture is polluted, but that usage is more literary.

distinctions.note: Dirty is an everyday word for something covered in dirt or marks; polluted refers to contamination by harmful substances, often from human activity.
Contaminated stresses that something has been made unsafe by an outside substance, often in food or water; polluted is more common for air, rivers and land.
Filthy is a strong word for extremely dirty things; polluted is more neutral and often used in environmental or health contexts.

examples.everyday: Don't let the kids swim in that lake, because the water is polluted after the storm.
examples.professional: The site was heavily polluted by decades of industrial solvent use, so we need a remediation plan before construction.
examples.analytical: Ethicists sometimes describe public discourse as polluted, but the metaphor can blur the difference between moral corruption and environmental harm.

nuance.analogy: Polluted air is like a room where someone has been burning incense for hours: everyone breathes it, whether they chose to or not.
nuance.etymology: From pollute, from Latin polluere, 'to defile', plus the suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the u as 'yoo' as in puh-LYOO-ted; General American uses 'oo', as in puh-LOO-tid.
Using polluted for ordinary dirt on a table or clothing, where dirty is the normal word.

senses.definition: A publication in several languages; specifically, a book (especially a bible) containing several versions of the same subject matter or text in several languages.
senses.example: The rare library edition was a polyglot Bible printed with Latin, Greek, and Hebrew columns side by side.

senses.definition: One who has mastered (especially when able to speak) several languages.
senses.example: My grandmother was a true polyglot who chatted comfortably with shopkeepers in six different languages.

senses.definition: A mixture of languages or nomenclatures.
senses.example: Her lecture was a polyglot of Latin jargon, street slang, and invented technical terms.

senses.definition: A file that can be interpreted validly as multiple formats.
senses.example: The security scanner flagged the upload as a polyglot because it opened as both a PDF and a ZIP.

senses.definition: A program written to be valid in multiple programming languages.
senses.example: The researcher wrote a polyglot script that parses correctly in Python, Perl, and C alike.

senses.definition: Of a person: speaking, or versed in, many languages; multilingual.
senses.example: Our polyglot tour guide switched effortlessly between Spanish, French, and English for every group.

senses.definition: Containing, or made up of, several languages; specifically, of a book (especially a bible): having text translated into several languages.
senses.example: a polyglot bible a polyglot lexicon

senses.definition: Comprising various (native) linguistic groups; multilingual.
senses.example: A polyglot region without a clearly dominant culture may develop an artificial lingua franca, such as Pidgin English in the South Sea.

core.definition: A person who speaks or reads several languages well.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is pronounced 'glaht', rhyming with 'lot', not 'glot' with a short o.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's language skill and intellectual range.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use polyglot mostly in writing or formal talk, such as describing a diplomat or a translator. In casual speech people more often say someone 'speaks a lot of languages' or is 'multilingual.' The adjective polyglot can describe a city or a book, such as a polyglot Bible that presents several translations side by side.

distinctions.note: Bilingual means speaking two languages, while polyglot suggests several languages and is more emphatic.
A linguist studies languages scientifically, while a polyglot is someone who uses many languages in practice.

examples.everyday: My coworker is a real polyglot, and she switches between Spanish and French on the phone.
examples.professional: We hired a polyglot support team so that customers can get help in six different languages.
examples.analytical: The polyglot scholar's commentary moves fluidly between Hebrew, Greek, and Latin sources, revealing shades of meaning that monolingual readers miss.

nuance.analogy: A polyglot is like a skilled musician who plays many instruments and switches between them with ease.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polyglottos, many-tongued, from polys, many, and glotta, tongue.
common_mistakes: Using polyglot as a verb or saying 'he polyglots' instead of 'he speaks several languages'
Confusing polyglot with the Greek-derived word for a linguist

senses.definition: The quality of being portable.
The ability of a program (or software system) to execute properly on multiple hardware platforms.
The ability of an employee to move between different social security schemes without losing their contributions.
senses.example: Thanks to portability, Maria's social security contributions carried over when she moved to Canada.

senses.definition: The ability of a telephone subscriber to keep their number when switching to a different network.
senses.example: Thanks to number portability, I kept my old phone number when I switched carriers.

core.definition: The ability of software to run correctly on different hardware platforms or operating systems without major changes.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'BIL', and the first syllable has a secondary stress. Reduce the vowels in the middle syllables, and do not stress the final '-ty', which sounds like 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; portability is valued because it saves time and money.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech teams, portability usually refers to software that runs on Windows, Mac and Linux, or on several cloud providers. Outside tech, Americans use it for the ability to carry or move something, such as a portable device. In benefits and retirement discussions, it can mean keeping pension credits when changing jobs.

distinctions.note: Compatibility means two systems work together, while portability means the same code can run on a new platform with little or no rewriting.
Mobility describes the ability to move or travel, while portability describes the ability to carry or transfer something, often a product or software.

examples.everyday: My sister chose that app because it works on her phone and her laptop, so the portability is a big plus.
examples.professional: We need to check the portability of the build pipeline before we move the service to a different cloud provider.
examples.analytical: The argument from portability assumes that the same concept can be applied across cultures without any loss of meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe that tastes the same whether you cook it in a small apartment kitchen or a large restaurant kitchen.
nuance.etymology: From portable, from Late Latin portabilis, from Latin portare 'to carry'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as 'pawr-tuh-bil-ih-TEE'.
Using 'portability' for a device that is merely small; in tech it means the code runs on different systems.

senses.definition: The edible starchy tuber of the plant species Solanum tuberosum.
senses.example: For dinner we roasted a tray of potatoes with rosemary and garlic.

senses.definition: The plant that produces this tuber.
senses.example: The potato in our community garden grew tall and flowered in early July.

senses.definition: A sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas).
senses.example: Grandma baked sweet potatoes with brown sugar and pecans for Thanksgiving.

senses.definition: A person or animal shaped like a potato, that is, with a large belly and/or short legs.
senses.example: Our puppy is a little potato with stubby legs and a round belly.

senses.definition: Metaphor for a person or thing of little value.
senses.example: The critics called the sequel a potato, not worth the price of a ticket.

senses.definition: A mentally handicapped person.
senses.example: Back then, the orderlies called residents like him potatoes, a cruel habit the new staff ended.

senses.definition: A camera that takes poor-quality pictures or videos.
senses.example: This phone camera is a potato, so the photos from the wedding came out grainy.

senses.definition: An underpowered computer or other device, especially when small in size.
senses.example: My old laptop is a potato, so I stopped running the model on it.

senses.definition: To hit very hard; to pummel.
senses.example: The linebacker potatoed the quarterback so hard that his helmet flew off.

senses.definition: To hit with a thrown or fired potato.
senses.example: Bored teenagers spent the summer potatoing parked cars from the hayfield behind the farm.

senses.definition: The rhythmic sound produced by a V-twin engine—a distinctive deep, throaty exhaust note.
senses.example: Potato, potato, potato, went the Harley as he rolled up to the stoplight.

core.definition: A starchy root vegetable that grows underground and is cooked and eaten as a side dish.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, TAY, and the final syllable is a light 'toh'. Americans do not add a secondary stress on the last syllable, and in fast speech the middle t often sounds like a soft flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly; 'couch potato' is a light, teasing label for someone who sits and watches TV a lot.
nuance.usage_note: Potato is very common in American kitchens and restaurants. Americans say 'fries' for French fries and 'chips' for thin crisp snacks, where British speakers say 'crisps'. In a restaurant you can ask for a baked or mashed potato as a side.

distinctions.note: A sweet potato is orange, purple, or yellow inside, comes from a different plant family, and tastes sweeter; a regular potato is starchier and usually white or yellow.
In American grocery stores, 'yams' are usually sweet potatoes; a true yam is a different tropical plant that is rarely sold in the US.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a few potatoes at the store? I want to make mashed potatoes for dinner.
examples.professional: The catering company added a potato salad option, so please confirm the headcount with them by Friday.
examples.analytical: The introduction of the potato to Europe reshaped diets and population growth, a point historians often emphasize.

nuance.analogy: A potato is the reliable workhorse of American dinners: plain, filling, and useful with almost anything.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish patata, from Taino batata, meaning 'sweet potato'.
common_mistakes: Using the plural 'potatos'; the correct plural is 'potatoes'.
Saying 'two potato' instead of 'two potatoes'; the noun is countable.

senses.definition: A barrel containing gunpowder.
An explosive or otherwise volatile situation.
senses.example: powder keg of Europe (term describing the unstable state of the Balkans before World War I)

core.definition: A barrel of gunpowder; figuratively, a situation that is likely to explode into violence or conflict.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'KEG' as the main word, with 'POW' lightly stressed. Say the 'er' in 'powder' quickly, and link the two words smoothly as 'POW-der KEG'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes danger or tension that could erupt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'powder keg' in news, politics, and everyday talk about tense situations, like 'the town is a powder keg'. It is a common idiom, not a literal term for most people. A natural reply to 'It's a powder keg in there' is 'Let's keep things calm'.

distinctions.note: Both mean a volatile situation; 'tinderbox' stresses that something small could start a fire, while 'powder keg' stresses a larger explosion.
A 'hot spot' is a place with conflict or activity; 'powder keg' implies the risk of sudden, violent explosion.

collocations: the region is a powder keg

examples.everyday: The neighborhood has been a powder keg since the zoning vote, so let's keep it quiet.
examples.professional: The budget dispute between the two teams is a powder keg, so let's bring in a neutral mediator before the next meeting.
examples.analytical: The alliance system, with its tangled suspicions, was a powder keg waiting for a single spark.

nuance.analogy: Like a barrel of gunpowder near an open flame, a tense situation can blow up with one small spark.
nuance.etymology: From powder (from Latin pulvis, 'dust') and keg, a small barrel.
common_mistakes: Using 'powder keg' for a literal keg of cosmetic powder; it is an idiom for danger.
Stressing 'keg' too weakly, which makes the phrase sound flat.

senses.definition: Synonym of magazine.
senses.example: The old fort's powder magazine stored gunpowder safely away from the barracks.

senses.definition: An individual or other situation that is bound to go awry or is potentially dangerous; a tinderbox.
senses.example: Their marriage had become a powder magazine, with every small argument threatening an explosion.

core.definition: A storehouse for gunpowder and other explosives; figuratively, a dangerous or volatile situation waiting to explode.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'POW' in 'powder' and 'MAG' in 'magazine'. The last syllable of 'magazine' in this sense is 'zeen', with a short middle vowel in 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; negative in figurative use, since it describes danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this phrase today except in historical writing, military history, or fort tours. In general talk people would say 'powder keg' or 'ammunition storage'. For a periodical, 'magazine' has a different pronunciation, so context matters.

distinctions.note: 'Powder keg' is the common idiom for a dangerous situation; 'powder magazine' is a historical or technical term for a storehouse.
An 'arsenal' is a place for weapons in general; a 'powder magazine' holds explosives specifically.

examples.everyday: We toured the old fort, and the guide showed us the stone powder magazine built into the hill.
examples.professional: Safety inspectors flagged the old powder magazine as unsafe, so the site was closed for repairs.
examples.analytical: The unresolved border dispute had turned the region into a powder magazine, where one incident could ignite a war.

nuance.analogy: A powder magazine is like a locked shed full of fireworks: safe only as long as nothing sparks near it.
nuance.etymology: From powder (from Latin pulvis, 'dust') and magazine, from Arabic makhazin, 'storehouses'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'magazine' as a storehouse with 'magazine' as a periodical, which has a different stress and meaning.
Using 'powder magazine' in everyday speech where 'powder keg' is more natural.

senses.definition: A device that converts direct current electricity to alternating current electricity.

core.definition: A device that converts direct current (DC) electricity, such as from a car battery, into alternating current (AC) electricity.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, POW gets the main stress and the -VUR- syllable of inverter has a secondary stress. The t between vowels is a quick flap that sounds like a soft d, so the word ends like 'in-VUR-der.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a practical technical term for a useful device.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use power inverter for the plug-in device that runs household electronics, like a laptop or small fridge, from a car's 12-volt socket, and for the larger units in home solar systems. In stores you will see it in the automotive aisle as a 'car power inverter.' In technical settings 'inverter' alone is common. Do not confuse it with a charger or adapter, which changes AC to DC.

distinctions.note: A converter changes electricity from one form to another, while an inverter specifically changes DC to AC; a phone charger is the opposite, an AC-to-DC converter.
A rectifier converts AC to DC, which is the reverse of what an inverter does.
An adapter usually changes the plug shape or voltage without changing the type of current; an inverter changes DC into AC.

collocations: plug a laptop into a power inverter
a pure sine wave power inverter

examples.everyday: I bought a power inverter so I can charge my laptop in the car on long road trips.
examples.professional: The solar system's power inverter converts the panel output from DC to grid-compatible AC, so we need to check its efficiency rating.
examples.analytical: The power inverter's efficiency determines how much of the battery's stored energy is actually delivered to the load as usable alternating current.

nuance.analogy: A power inverter is like a translator who turns one language into another so that different systems can understand each other.
nuance.etymology: Power from Old French poeir, from Latin potere, 'to be able'; inverter from Latin invertere, 'to turn upside down.'
common_mistakes: Confusing an inverter with a charger or converter; a charger turns AC into DC, the opposite direction.
Stressing IN-verter as if inverter were the first word; in this compound, POW- gets the main stress.

senses.definition: Initialism of public relations.
Initialism of proportional representation.
Initialism of permanent residence.
Initialism of police report.
Initialism of personal representative.
Initialism of personal recognizance (bond).
Initialism of personal record.
Initialism of purchase requisition.
Initialism of pull request.
Initialism of protected ranking.
Initialism of Puerto Rican.
Initialism of progesterone receptor.
Initialism of partial response.
Initialism of prothrombin ratio.
A PR interval.
Abbreviation of preset.
Initialism of Paralympic record.
Initialism of per-rectal or per rectum.
(uncommon) To perform public relations work, such as promoting or managing publicity for something.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: Public relations: the work of managing how the public, media and customers see a company, person or organization.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters P and R, with primary stress on the R (AR) and a lighter stress on P. The R is strongly rhotic, so do not drop it or make it a vowel like 'pee-ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a professional function, but people may use it negatively when they mean spin or damage control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the letters 'P-R' for public relations in business, news, and everyday conversation. Context matters: in software, PR means pull request, and in some contexts it can mean proportional representation or permanent residence.
